projectDetails.name: AstroFire 3D
projectDetails.summary:
AstroFire 3D is an interactive fire safety console, 3D Unity WebGL simulator, and Super Intelligence (SI) copilot built on open NASA space combustion data.

On Earth, hot air rises and gives fire a teardrop shape, but in space flames form quiet blue spheres that behave very differently. Standard ground tests miss these risks, and NASA’s data is scattered across technical databases (PSI and NTRS). To solve this, we built a physics engine grounded on 79 verified BASS-II tests from the ISS (R² = 0.91 for flame-spread prediction). We then added 71 more ISS flight states to train a physics-informed neural network that predicts whether a flame survives, reaching 95.3% cross-validated accuracy and catching 97.7% of sustained fires. We also rank six NASA campaigns (BASS-II, Saffire, SoFIE, SAME, FLEX and SPICE) by relevance to four space habitats.

Users test 7 real NASA materials across the ISS (0g), Moon (0.16g), Mars (0.38g), and Earth (1g), adjusting oxygen and airflow to see burn speed, minimum oxygen limit, CO and CO₂ gases, live 3D flame behavior, and generate an analysis report. As an extra feature, we integrated microgravity heat transfer research from Brazil, our homeland, to size water-mist extinguisher suppression. Every result separates direct NASA data from estimates, supporting safer space missions and fire safety on Earth.

Make the next giant leap safer!

projectDetails.name: CORA - Crew Operations Readiness Assistant
projectDetails.summary:
CORA (Crew Operations Readiness Assistant) is an onboard-first health telemetry prototype for space crews. It combines simulated wearable signals, manual measurements, daily check-ins, personal pre-flight baselines, and historical NASA environmental references to provide an explainable next operational action.

The system collects and evaluates local evidence even when communication with Earth is unavailable. It distinguishes normal, deviating, stale, invalid, and missing data; recommends actions such as routine monitoring, rechecking a measurement, or reviewing before a critical task; and safely synchronizes queued evidence with Earth once the link returns.

CORA addresses the challenge by helping astronauts monitor relevant health indicators, assess their own readiness, and act without waiting for ground support. This is important for long-duration missions, where isolation, distance, delayed communication, and environmental hazards make local autonomy essential.
projectDetails.details:
CORA is a health-monitoring platform for astronauts designed to keep working even when communication with Earth is limited or unavailable.

The idea started with a simple question: if an astronaut notices a change in their health during a mission, what can they do while waiting for support from the ground team? To explore this, we created a system that brings together simulated wearable data, daily check-ins, and manual health entries.

Instead of only displaying numbers, CORA compares current readings with each astronaut’s personal pre-flight baseline. This helps identify when something is unusual for that individual and provides a clear operational suggestion: continue the routine, monitor the situation, or review their status before a critical task.

The main feature of the project is that it continues working onboard without an Earth connection. Data is stored locally and, once the link is restored, it is safely synchronized with a ground-team dashboard. This prevents information loss and helps the team understand what happened during the communication gap.

We built CORA using Python and FastAPI for the onboard and Earth services, PostgreSQL for data storage, and React with TypeScript for the interface. We also created a wearable simulator and used Docker to run the full system.

CORA is not intended to diagnose diseases or replace medical professionals. It is a demonstration of how health data, personal context, and resilient communication can help astronauts make more informed decisions during long, isolated missions with delayed contact with Earth.

projectDetails.name: Earth Information Jukebox — Angular Lovers
projectDetails.summary:
Earth Information Jukebox is an interactive web experience developed by Angular Lovers to make NASA Earth science more engaging through sight, sound, and exploration.

Inspired by NASA's Earth Information Center, our application transforms real nighttime satellite imagery into music generated in real time. Users can explore an interactive globe, select NASA night-lights images from 2012 or 2023, and listen as visual brightness is translated into musical notes. A synchronized visual indicator and textual descriptions explain how each region contributes to the sound.

Built with Angular, TypeScript, Canvas2D, and the Web Audio API, the project combines scientific visualization with a reproducible sound-generation system. Its purpose is to explore new ways of communicating Earth information, supporting multisensory learning and making complex visual material more approachable.

By turning images into an interactive musical experience, we invite people to discover our changing planet from a different perspective.

projectDetails.name: ARARA — Radar Water Monitor
projectDetails.summary: ARARA turns NISAR, the NASA–ISRO L-band radar satellite, into a water-change monitor that anyone can read. Floods, droughts and reservoir swings often happen under clouds, exactly when optical satellites are blind; radar measures water day or night, in any weather. For each monitored area, ARARA reads every NISAR pass, separates water from land and compares it with the driest pass of the period, showing where water advanced or retreated, how much, which municipalities were affected and how much it rained before, each number with a confidence level. When the radar cannot separate water from land, ARARA says so instead of showing a number. The pipeline is region-agnostic; we deployed it first in southern Brazil, a region hit by recurring floods, and validated it against official data from Brazil's National Water Agency (ANA): flood area in Porto Alegre tracks the official river gauge (r = 0.95 on 5 of 6 passes, same peak date), and reservoir area at Furnas matches ANA's official level–area curve within 1%. The pass-by-pass water history ARARA builds helps find the areas that flood first and can feed flood-prediction models.
projectDetails.details:
The problem

Water changes — floods, droughts, reservoirs filling and emptying — shape the lives of millions of people, but the worst moments usually happen under heavy clouds and rain, exactly when optical satellites cannot see the ground. River gauges measure the water level at one point, not where the water spread. Civil defence, river-basin committees, reservoir operators and city halls need to know where water advanced or retreated, how far, and who was affected. Radar can see through clouds, but its data is hard to access and interpret.

What ARARA does

ARARA is a water-change monitor built on NISAR, the NASA–ISRO L-band synthetic aperture radar, which measures water day or night, with or without clouds. For each monitored area, ARARA:

• reads each NISAR pass over the area and separates water from land;

• compares every pass with the driest calm pass of the period and maps the extra water (flood) or the water lost, counted only on low terrain;

• flags possible flooded vegetation, adds the rainfall of the previous days (NASA GPM IMERG) and lists the affected municipalities with their population;

• gives every number a confidence level with its reasons (wind, coverage, agreement with Sentinel-2);

• writes a plain-language summary generated from the numbers.

The interactive globe ranks the monitored areas by measured flood area. Each area has a pass-by-pass timeline, a slider that compares any pass with the driest one, the municipalities affected at the peak, a downloadable history (CSV) and an automatic full study. When the radar cannot separate water from land, ARARA says so and publishes no number instead of a wrong one.

Where we applied it

The processing pipeline does not depend on a specific place: an area is a configuration, and the same method measures rivers, floodplains and reservoirs. We deployed it first where it matters most to us: southern Brazil, a region hit by recurring floods, with nine flood-prone areas monitored in Rio Grande do Sul, Santa Catarina and Paraná, plus reservoir studies in Minas Gerais and on the Brazil–Uruguay river basin.

Validation against official data

• Porto Alegre (Guaíba): NISAR flood area vs. the official ANA river gauge 87450020 at the time of each pass: r = 0.95 on 5 of 6 passes (August–October 2026), with the flood peak on the same date as the river peak (3 October). One pass diverges (low river, more water detected, after 85 mm of rain); it is documented, not hidden.

• Furnas reservoir (Minas Gerais): NISAR water area vs. ANA's official level–area curve at the official daily level: 1.0% mean absolute error on 7 calm dates; sensitivity of 47 km²/m measured vs. 45 km²/m in the official curve.

• Barra Grande and Machadinho reservoirs, experimental: NISAR caught two reservoirs rising 14 m and 9 m in 12 days of winter rain, on the right dates (r = 0.98 and 0.85), but underestimates the area in these narrow canyons. We publish it as experimental, with the reason.

Benefits and intended impact

ARARA turns open NASA radar data into a water history that a city, a basin committee or a reservoir operator can read: where water arrived or receded, when, and which municipalities were exposed. Repeated passes build a record of the places that flood first, which can guide prevention and feed flood-prediction models. Because radar does not depend on clear skies, it fills the gap exactly when optical images fail — in any cloudy, flood-prone region of the world.

Creativity and what we considered

Instead of a pretty map, ARARA treats trust as a feature: every number is measured, has a confidence level and a validation path, and the app prefers "unmeasured" to a wrong number. We separated measurement from cause (radar says where there is extra water, not why), checked every claim against official data (ANA, ONS, IBGE), and kept the results reproducible: data, scripts and regression results are in the repository.

Limitations

• NISAR products are still provisional; our series start in June 2026.

• A flood that lasts the whole period is invisible, because it is part of the reference (the driest pass).

• Smooth land (rice fields, marshes) can look like water to the radar; in five of the nine monitored areas the radar did not separate water from land, and ARARA shows no number there.

• The Porto Alegre gauge series used for validation starts in mid-August 2026.

Tools

Python (NumPy, SciPy, h5py, rasterio and related libraries) for the NISAR processing pipeline; Java 21 and Spring Boot with PostgreSQL for the API and the pass-by-pass history; JavaScript with Leaflet and globe.gl for the interactive globe and maps; Docker, Caddy and Traefik for hosting. Data from NASA Earthdata / ASF DAAC (NISAR L2 GCOV), NASA GPM IMERG, ANA, ONS, IBGE, Copernicus Sentinel-2 and GLO-30 HAND.

Use of AI

We used AI tools (Anthropic's Claude) as assistants: to help us understand the NISAR data (product structure, HDF5 layout, radar concepts such as backscatter and decibel conversion), to help build the application (code, tests, documentation and review) and to help edit the demo video. The interpretation of the problem and the idea behind ARARA are our own: tracking water with radar, the choice of floods and reservoirs as first use cases, and validating against official data. AI-assisted outputs were reviewed and tested by the team, and all reported results come from real NISAR data processed by our pipeline.

• Demo video: edited with AI assistance and marked with a visible "AI-assisted edit" watermark; its background music and sound effects were generated with AI-assisted code; the narration is our own voice.

• ARARA logo: created with AI assistance.

projectDetails.name: AETHER: Mission Architect
projectDetails.summary: AETHER: Mission Architect is an interactive educational game that allows users to experience the challenges of designing a space mission. Players take on the role of mission architects, making strategic decisions about scientific objectives, mass, power, communications, orbital constraints, reliability, and budget. Each decision affects the mission's performance and overall success. By transforming complex aerospace engineering concepts into an engaging simulation, AETHER makes space exploration more accessible and encourages critical thinking, problem-solving, and scientific curiosity. The project aims to inspire students and aspiring engineers to understand the real-world trade-offs involved in planning successful space missions.
projectDetails.details: Sobre o Projeto AETHER: Mission Architect é um simulador interativo de engenharia aeroespacial desenvolvido durante o NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026. projectDetails.name: Project Artemis Adventure
projectDetails.summary: Artemis Adventure is a short, decision-making game set at an outpost on the Moon. Players take on the role of a junior commander on their first 5-day mission. Each day, players must choose two actions such as cleaning solar panels, adjusting life-support systems, or preparing shields since it is impossible to do everything. Four resources must be managed: energy, oxygen, food, and health, all of which directly impact the success of the mission. The game also features emergencies, such as solar storms, based on real-world events recorded in NASA’s DONKI database. Through the consequences of their own choices, players learn how resource scarcity, radiation, and careful planning shape life on the Moon. Our solution addresses the challenge by blending science with fun, transforming complex concepts into a hands-on adventure for children aged 7 to 12. Our goal goes beyond simple instruction, we aim to inspire the next generation of scientists and explorers from an early age.
projectDetails.details:
Game Overview

Before starting, players choose a landing site. There are three options inspired by candidate regions for the Artemis missions: the Sunlit Crater Rim, the Shadowed South Pole, and the Central Plains. Each location has its own advantages and risks, as well as determining when lunar night begins and which resources are available at the start of the mission.

1. Morning Briefing

Mission Control presents the tasks for the day, including the cost and potential reward of each activity. It also provides important warnings, such as an approaching lunar night or a solar storm forecast for the following day.

2. Base Modules

The game takes place on a lunar base composed of five modules: Life Support, Greenhouse, Bunker, Power, and Habitat.

3. Completing Tasks

Each task is an interactive minigame. Examples include cleaning and adjusting the orientation of solar panels, calibrating batteries, replacing CO2 filters, cultivating algae, watering plants, preparing meals, removing lunar dust, and reinforcing the base's shielding.

Performance is essential: with up to 20% error, the player receives the full reward. Above that threshold, the reward decreases, while excessive mistakes result in losing the task entirely.

4. Resource Indicators

The game features four main indicators: Energy, Food, Oxygen, and Health.

Every night, the base consumes supplies. If any resource falls below 25, the crew's health begins to deteriorate. If a resource reaches zero, the mission is aborted.

5. Space Weather Events and Emergencies

Emergencies occur randomly throughout the mission.

  • Solar Storm: Modeled using real events from NASA's DONKI database.
  • Meteor Shower: A randomly selected module is targeted, and the player has 20 seconds to activate the emergency lever.
  • Navigation Computer: Provides access to space weather information, the mission log, forecasts, base status, and real DONKI data.

6. Learning Through Gameplay

Each minigame begins with a tutorial card explaining a real-world scientific fact about why astronauts perform that activity, with information sourced from NASA or ESA.

The first time players enter a module, an introductory card explains its purpose and presents a relevant scientific fact and its source.

7. Final Mission Report

At the end of the mission, players receive a summary of their results, a timeline highlighting the most important moments based on their most impactful decisions and the trade-offs involved, and information about the real NASA DONKI event used as the basis for that playthrough.

Benefits

  1. Learning by Doing: Players understand firsthand how energy, air, food, and health depend on one another.
  2. Scientific Content with Reliable Sources: The game includes 20 real scientific facts, each connected to NASA or ESA data and sources. Solar storms also use real data from NASA's DONKI API.
  3. Accessibility: The game runs directly in a computer's web browser.

Impact

Our goal is to bring children aged 7–12, as well as the general public, closer to space missions and the realities of living and working on the Moon.

We teach systems thinking and decision-making by allowing players to experience the consequences of their choices, which directly influence the success of the mission.

The game can also be used as a complementary educational tool in the classroom. Our game goes beyond simple instruction: we aim to inspire the next generation of scientists and explorers from an early age.

Tools and Technologies

Game Development

  • Godot Engine with GDScript.
  • JSON for data storage and management.

Art and Audio

  • Pixel art using a unified palette (APOLLO).
  • Python Pillow for art processing and generation scripts.

NASA Data and Scientific Sources

  • NASA DONKI.
  • NASA API (api.nasa.gov).
  • NASA Technical Reports Server (NTRS).

Development and Collaboration

  • Git and GitHub.
  • Balancing bots developed in GDScript.

Use of Artificial Intelligence

Claude Code: Used as a programming assistant to help write and review code.

Local Image Generation Pipeline: Used to generate artwork for the rooms, minigames, cards, and title screen. The generated images were then converted into pixel art using the APOLLO palette and refined manually or through scripts. Some assets, such as the astronaut, were drawn pixel by pixel.

Factors Considered by the Team

Scope for a 48-Hour Development Period

Our initial plan was designed for a seven-day development period, with 10 rooms and 19 minigames. We reduced the scope to five days, five rooms, and 15 minigames, prioritizing a complete and polished game over a larger prototype.

Scientific Accuracy

Every scientific fact was verified against NASA or ESA sources, and solar events are obtained directly from DONKI.

Learning Curve and Accessibility

Tutorials before each minigame and a morning briefing displaying the cost and reward of each task help players understand the mechanics and make informed decisions.

Game Balancing

The game was tested using balancing bots designed to simulate different types of players: smart, average, random, and clumsy players.

projectDetails.summary:
**Outpost** is an interactive educational simulator designed to explore the challenges of human survival in space environments. The project places users in the role of an astronaut, allowing them to interact with the systems of a fictional space outpost.

The platform features resource management, an interactive cockpit, piloting missions, and a multilingual interface, combining exploration, decision-making, and educational experiences.

Its main objective is to introduce users to the technological and operational challenges involved in establishing and maintaining human habitats beyond Earth. By transforming space exploration concepts into an interactive experience, Outpost encourages curiosity about science, engineering, technology, and the future of human space exploration.

The project aims to make space-related learning more accessible, engaging, and immersive.
projectDetails.details:
1. What the Project Does and How It Works

Outpost is an interactive space survival and exploration simulator designed to introduce users to the challenges of living and operating in space environments.

Users take on the role of an astronaut and interact with a simulated space outpost through different features, including resource management systems, an interactive cockpit, piloting missions, and multilingual interface options.

The simulator combines interactive elements with educational concepts related to space exploration, encouraging users to make decisions and understand the complexity of operating a space habitat.

2. Benefits and Expected Impact

Outpost aims to make space exploration concepts more accessible and engaging, particularly for students and people interested in science, technology, engineering, and space exploration.

Its educational approach encourages curiosity, critical thinking, problem-solving, and awareness of the challenges associated with human space missions.

The intended impact is to create an accessible learning experience that helps users better understand the responsibilities and difficulties involved in maintaining human presence beyond Earth.

3. Technologies and Development Tools

The project was developed using web technologies:

  • HTML5: Structure and organization of the simulator.
  • CSS3: Visual design, interface styling, and responsive elements.
  • JavaScript: Interactive functionality and simulator mechanics.
  • GitHub: Source code management and project collaboration.
  • GitHub Pages: Public hosting and deployment.

Artificial intelligence tools, including ChatGPT (OpenAI) and Claude (Anthropic), were also used to support brainstorming, programming, debugging, problem-solving, and documentation.

4. Creative Aspects

The main creative aspect of Outpost is its combination of an educational experience with interactive space simulation.

Instead of presenting space exploration exclusively through static information, the project allows users to experience selected aspects of astronaut activities through a simulated environment.

The combination of resource management, cockpit interaction, piloting missions, and multilingual accessibility creates an engaging approach to introducing space-related concepts.

5. Design Considerations and Development Decisions

During development, the team considered usability, accessibility, educational value, and technical feasibility.

The interface was designed to provide an understandable experience while maintaining a space exploration aesthetic. The multilingual functionality was included to make the simulator accessible to a broader audience.

The team also considered the importance of creating an experience that could run through a web browser without requiring specialized hardware or software installation.

Outpost represents an educational exploration of the challenges of human spaceflight, combining interactive web development with an interest in the future of space exploration.

projectDetails.details:
This project is a cardiovascular health monitoring software designed for astronauts on space missions to other planets and/or natural satellites. It is based on the Ankle-Brachial Index (ABI) examination, which assesses general and peripheral cardiovascular health, as well as the risk of serious cardiovascular events—such as myocardial infarction (heart attack) and stroke—to help guide the prescription of physical exercise aimed at preventing health complications in astronauts.

The project is founded on the principle that the space environment triggers vascular adaptations that mimic the premature aging of arteries. Studies indicate that six months in space leads to arterial narrowing, reflecting a loss of elasticity similar to that observed in the early stages of atherosclerosis. As a countermeasure, we have developed this software to assist astronauts in performing the examination, interpreting results, tracking clinical progress, managing cardiovascular rehabilitation (if necessary), and maintaining overall health.

The software features a simple, interactive interface that provides detailed health and risk indicators. Data can be entered using a keyboard and mouse. The examination process is straightforward, thanks to the portability and simplicity of the required equipment, making it highly practical for use in space environments. The results generated by the software can inform decision-making for both the crew and the medical team on Earth.

Our goal is to make a positive impact on space missions by enabling astronauts to spend longer periods in extraterrestrial environments without compromising their health, thereby expanding the scope and ensuring the success of these missions. Furthermore, the software aims to mitigate health-related impacts for astronauts on current and future missions.

This project was developed using Python 3, HTML, CSS, JavaScript, and SVG. We use the artificial intelligence Claude AI to assist in searching for information and writing code. This includes accessing resources such as NASA databases—covering human research and physical exercise equipment—as well as scientific articles available through the space agency’s partners and other data sources.

Our project takes a creative approach by integrating knowledge from the fields of computing, cardiovascular health, physical exercise, and space engineering to develop innovative software designed for the identification, promotion, maintenance, and rehabilitation of cardiovascular health.

Our team is currently examining topics such as cardiovascular health and the ankle-brachial index; human health data in space environments; issues related to gravitational differences between planets and their impact on human physiology; the effects of space travel and microgravity environments; the adverse effects experienced by astronauts during and after space missions; equipment and strategies for maintaining health in space; and existing or potential digital tools and devices for use during space missions.

projectDetails.details:
BRASPACE — Lunar Landing Site Navigator

Project Overview

BRASPACE is developing an interactive web-based tool to help users explore and compare potential lunar landing sites near the Moon's south pole.

The project addresses two critical challenges in lunar surface exploration: solar illumination for energy generation and direct-to-Earth visibility for communication.

Our objective is to make these complex scientific considerations easier to understand through an accessible interface, transparent indicators, and a reproducible software architecture.

The Problem

The Moon's south pole presents unique operational challenges. Low solar elevation angles, terrain shadows, and local horizon obstructions can strongly affect surface illumination and communication conditions.

Choosing an appropriate landing location requires understanding how these conditions change across different sites and dates.

Scientific tools exist, but their complexity can limit accessibility for students, educators, and people exploring preliminary mission-design concepts.

Our Approach

The Lunar Landing Site Navigator offers a browser-based interface for exploring candidate locations and comparing simplified site indicators.

Users can select a date, inspect available candidate locations, and review illustrative estimates related to solar elevation, Earth visibility, and comparative suitability.

The interface is designed to emphasize understandable results and explainable trade-offs rather than presenting an unexplained ranking.

Software Architecture

The prototype uses a modular architecture consisting of:

Go: HTTP API, request handling, candidate-site access, and comparison endpoints.

Rust: An independent geometry component for reusable mathematical calculations.

PostgreSQL: Database infrastructure for storing lunar site information and future scientific datasets.

pgvector: Infrastructure for potential semantic and similarity-based retrieval of site metadata.

Docker and Docker Compose: Reproducible application configuration.

HTML, CSS, and JavaScript: Responsive frontend implementation.

The current Go API uses an in-memory site catalog. The Rust engine and PostgreSQL database have been prepared as separate components but are not yet integrated into the API's main calculation workflow.

Current Prototype

The current MVP includes an interactive browser interface, backend API endpoints, a separate computational component, and containerization files.

Its numerical results are simplified educational estimates. They are not terrain-aware, mission-grade predictions.

In particular, the current version does not yet implement validated NASA ephemerides, high-resolution lunar horizon profiles, or physically verified communication-window calculations.

These limitations are disclosed explicitly to avoid overstating the system's scientific capabilities.

NASA Data Integration Roadmap

The next scientific development phase focuses on integrating authoritative NASA lunar exploration resources, including Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter data and Lunar Orbiter Laser Altimeter products.

Our intended methodology is to:

  1. Obtain and document authoritative lunar terrain datasets.
  2. Construct horizon profiles around selected candidate locations.
  3. Calculate solar and Earth directions using verified astronomical geometry.
  4. Evaluate visibility relative to the local terrain horizon.
  5. Generate time-dependent illumination and communication windows.
  6. Compare locations using documented and reproducible criteria.
  7. Validate numerical results against independent references.

Innovation

BRASPACE combines a user-centered visual experience with a modular engineering architecture.

The project's primary innovation is its focus on making the trade-offs of lunar landing-site selection more accessible and explainable.

The architecture is designed to support future additions such as interactive terrain visualization, time-series comparisons, scientific provenance, and more advanced search capabilities.

Intended Impact

We want students, educators, space enthusiasts, and researchers to understand why a promising lunar landing site must be evaluated across multiple environmental and operational dimensions.

A future scientifically validated version could support early exploration of potential landing sites and encourage more informed discussions about lunar surface missions.

Transparency and Responsible Use of AI

Generative AI assisted the development workflow through ideation, software scaffolding, code generation, documentation, and project-submission drafting.

The team remains responsible for reviewing all generated material and validating technical and scientific claims.

AI assistance does not establish scientific correctness.

The project is an independent hackathon submission and is not a NASA-approved mission planning system.

projectDetails.name: HORIZON
projectDetails.summary: HORIZON is an educational project made of two connected browser games that teach children aged 7 to 12 how a Mars base really works. In Mission Jezero, a 3D globe built from real NASA images (Viking, MRO CTX and HiRISE) leads players to Jezero Crater, where they build a base and decide each sol how to split power between air, shielding and science. In Arcadia Colony, they become the commander on the surface: going out on EVA, building with Martian resources, and protecting the crew from solar storms, marsquakes and dust. The project addresses the challenge by covering life support, radiation protection, power, food, water and communication delay, with NASA data driving every decision: live DONKI space weather triggers solar alerts, and real results from Curiosity, Perseverance’s MOXIE, InSight and Phoenix shape the rules. It matters because space content for kids is often abstract or too technical, showing results but never the reasoning behind them. Here, every choice has a real cost explained on screen, so children learn by trying, failing and thinking like engineers.
projectDetails.details: HORIZON is an educational browser game for children aged 7 to 12, made of two connected parts. In Mission Jezero, a 3D globe built from real NASA images (Viking MDIM 2.1, MRO CTX and HiRISE, via NASA Mars Trek) takes the player down to Jezero Crater. There they found a base and act as mission control, splitting each sol’s power between air, shielding and science after seeing a forecast. In Arcadia Colony, they become the commander on the surface: they go out on EVA through the airlock, build with Martian resources such as regolith, ice and iron, manage food, water and oxygen, and protect the crew from solar storms, marsquakes, meteorites and dust. Live space weather from NASA’s DONKI decides when solar alerts happen, which real event they come from and when the cloud reaches Mars. HORIZON turns abstract space science into decisions children can feel: every choice has a real cost explained on screen, and a “go back 1 sol” button lets a class compare strategies. It runs in any browser with no download or sign-up, so it works on ordinary school computers, tablets and phones. Our intended impact is to teach the reasoning behind space missions, not just their results, so children learn that saving power today can cost oxygen tomorrow and come to see engineering and NASA data as tools for making decisions. We built it with HTML, CSS and JavaScript, Three.js (WebGL) for 3D, TypeScript, React and Vite on the Lovable platform, and Node.js for automated tests. It uses the NASA DONKI API and NASA Mars Trek image tiles, CC0 assets from Kenney and Poly Haven, and is hosted on Netlify. The code, texts and 3D visuals were generated with generative AI (Anthropic Claude and Lovable AI) under the team’s direction, as declared in AI-USE.md. The creative side lies in two linked views of one mission, in solar alerts that can be false alarms (the real dilemma of a flight director), in building the colony from Martian materials, and in natural disasters that come from our own Java disaster simulator. We designed it for its age group, with simple language, a glossary, a guide character and a Cadet Mode with only three resources. We kept every number scientifically honest and cited its source, made sure it runs on low-end devices and is fun to replay, respected NASA’s brand rules by crediting without logos, and disclosed our AI use openly.

projectDetails.name: CheeseOS
projectDetails.summary:
CheeseOS is an autonomous health system for astronauts, built for missions where a doctor isn’t just a click away. The astronaut interacts with a 3D human body and uses their voice to describe what they feel and where. The system interprets the report, pinpoints the symptom on the 3D model, and instantly returns clear, practical care guidance.

Monitoring health in space gets harder with every mission. On trips to the Moon and Mars, communication with Earth can be delayed by several minutes or even lost entirely, so waiting for a doctor’s response isn’t always an option. CheeseOS solves this by giving astronauts an immediate answer without relying on anyone on the ground. At the same time, every report is logged, and medical teams on Earth can review this history later to follow the crew’s health throughout the mission.

This matters because the farther humanity travels, the more autonomous the crew needs to be. CheeseOS is a step in that direction.
projectDetails.details:
What it does and how it works
CheeseOS is an autonomous health twin for astronauts on long-duration missions. On the way to Mars a message can take up to 20 minutes each way, so the first answer has to come from the system itself. The astronaut says or types how they feel, the app recognizes the symptoms on the device, lights up the affected region on a 3D body and shows the onboard protocol step by step. Every report goes into a log that reaches the medical team on Earth as soon as the link allows, so doctors can review the case and send back a deeper assessment. Voice input was designed to be built into the helmet, so the guidance follows the astronaut even during a spacewalk.

A tour of the system

1. Onboarding
The first launch builds the astronaut's digital twin in three short steps (identification, body and health). This data stays on the device and gives the system the context it needs before any guidance, such as allergies and medications in use.

2. Now, talk or tap where it hurts
The home screen asks a single question, how are you? The astronaut taps the microphone (or presses the space bar) and speaks, types, or touches the point on the 3D body where it hurts. The same screen holds today's missions (health check-in, vitals review, exercise and hydration), the check-in streak and a one tap sleep log that warns when the weekly average drops under 7 hours.

3. Instant guidance
As soon as a symptom is reported, the screen turns into an action plan. Each card is a numbered step of the onboard protocol, sorted by severity, with a "Why in space?" note that explains the link to spaceflight. The astronaut marks each step as gone or not this, and the 3D twin glows on the affected regions.

4. Critical mode
When red flags appear, such as chest pain with shortness of breath, local rules raise a critical state without depending on any AI. The most urgent steps move to the top in red (stop the activity, run an ECG, check cabin O2 and CO2, call the flight surgeon) and the vital signs out of range are highlighted below.

5. Body map
The History area has a full body map. Symptoms appear on seven regions with a heat scale (no complaints, mild, attention, critical), and a side list shows each region with its active symptoms, guidance and previous reports.

6. Vital signs
Temperature, blood pressure, respiration, heart rate and SpO2, each with its reference range, attention and critical limits and a live chart. In this demo the values are simulated and react to the reported symptoms. In a real mission they would come from wearable sensors in the suit.

7. Log and export for the flight surgeon
Every voice or text report is saved with its time and tagged symptoms, next to a symptom timeline. With one click the astronaut exports a complete report (profile, safety alerts, active symptoms and protocol, vital signs from the last hour and the full log) as text or as a printable HTML/PDF for the medical team on Earth.

8. Training
Exercise is the main countermeasure against bone and muscle loss in microgravity. CheeseOS offers six resistive and aerobic exercises, and the camera counts repetitions and checks range of motion on the device with MediaPipe. No video is recorded or sent. The screen tracks on how many of the last 7 days the countermeasure was done, compared with the ISS routine of 6 to 7 days a week.

9. Crew profile
Blood type, allergies, medications in use, previous conditions and body measurements. This is what the crew and the AI need to know before any action, and the system uses it to block medications that conflict with the astronaut's allergies.

10. Mission science
A page that connects the symptoms to the five hazards of NASA's Human Research Program (gravity fields, hostile and closed environment, radiation, isolation and confinement, distance from Earth). Each hazard shows its countermeasures, the symptoms currently linked to it and its sources, followed by a table with every limit the app uses and where it comes from.

11. Settings and privacy
The astronaut chooses the AI engine (OpenRouter, a small model running on the device, or no AI at all with only the local rules), the language (Portuguese or English), local reminders and a demo mode that speeds up the simulation. Voice transcription runs on the device with Whisper, and the audio never leaves it.

Benefits
Astronauts get immediate help without waiting for mission control. They choose how to communicate: typing inside the spacecraft, or speaking when their hands are busy or they are suited up. With voice in the helmet, support doesn’t stop at the hatch and follows the astronaut on spacewalks, one of the highest risk moments for injury. The 3D model makes reports more precise, since showing where it hurts is easier than explaining it. And care happens in two layers: instant guidance from the system, followed by detailed feedback from doctors on the ground, who also gain a continuous view of the crew’s health.

Factors the team considered
Communication delays and blackouts with Earth, which is why the first guidance has to come from the system itself. Ease of use under stress, since someone who is hurt needs something simple. Flexible input, with voice and text for different situations. The limitations of the spacesuit, which make using hands difficult and led to the idea of voice in the helmet. Clear guidance that any crew member can follow, even without medical training. And continuity of care, with everything logged so the medical team on the ground can analyze it and build on the initial guidance.

Tools and technologies
Next.js 16, React 19 and TypeScript for the app. Three.js with React Three Fiber for the 3D twin. transformers.js running Whisper on the device for speech recognition. MediaPipe Tasks Vision for repetition counting. Tailwind CSS 4 for the interface and Vitest for tests. Optional AI through OpenRouter or a local model, always on top of deterministic safety rules. NASA Human Research Program references and NIH MedlinePlus vital sign ranges ground the protocols and limits.

Use of AI
We used AI tools to support the team during the hackathon. ChatGPT was used to create the CheeseOS logo. Claude Code (Anthropic) was used to write code, plan the project and organize and refine our written texts. Claude was also used to edit the project video. All AI output was reviewed, tested and adjusted by the team.

projectDetails.name: Project CosmoHealth
projectDetails.summary:
AstroHealth is a desktop app written in Python (Tkinter, no installation needed) that monitors astronaut health on space missions. It was created for the NASA Space Apps challenge.
The core idea is to compare each astronaut with their **own normal**, rather than a general average. The app tracks five indicators: heart rate, SpO2, sleep, exercise and radiation. A traffic light (green, yellow and red) warns early when something starts to change and recommends the right action. The data is simulated in three scenarios (Normal, Gradual decline and Emergency) or typed in by the user.
The dashboard shows an animated ECG, a health index, trends, radiation dose and a measurement history. The Mission tab offers animated scenes of the ISS, the Moon and Mars, with the communication delay and the autonomous protocol. In the logbook, the astronaut describes their day, and the simulated medical officer analyzes the text and gives an opinion, such as rest and kit medication for a fever.
There is also a crew overview, light and dark mode, TXT and CSV export, and automatic saving.
The data is fictional and the app does not replace a medical evaluation. The logbook keywords are still in Portuguese.
projectDetails.details:
O que faz e como funciona: AstroHealth é um aplicativo de desktop que monitora a saúde dos astronautas em missões espaciais. Ele rastreia a frequência cardíaca, SpO2, sono, exercício e radiação, e compara cada astronauta com seus próprio normal em vez de uma média geral. Um semáforo (verde, amarelo e vermelho) avisa cedo quando algo começa a mudar e mostra a ação recomendada. No diário de bordo, o astronauta descreve o seu dia com as suas próprias palavras. O texto é analisado juntamente com as medidas, e um médico simulado emite uma opinião com o curso de ação recomendado, como repouso, hidratação e medicação em kit para febre.

Benefícios: Detecção precoce de problemas, orientação imediata e registro organizado de medições, relatórios e eventos da tripulação.

Impacto pretendido: Em missões longas, como Marte, uma resposta da Terra leva minutos. O aplicativo dá aos astronautas autonomia para perceber mudanças e agir por conta própria, além de dar ao controle de solo uma visão clara de toda a tripulação.

Ferramentas: Python e Tkinter (biblioteca padrão, sem dependências), JSON para salvar dados e CSV/TXT para exportar. Não usamos hardware. Os dados são simulados em três cenários (Normal, Declínio Gradual e Emergência) ou digitados pelo usuário.

Criatividade: Uma normal pessoal em vez de uma média geral, alertas baseados em tendências antes que um valor saia do intervalo seguro, um diário de bordo analisado por regras (ele entende negações e lê números no texto) e cenas animadas da ISS, da Lua e de Marte com atrasos de comunicação realistas.

Fatores considerados: Microgravidade, isolamento, radiação, atraso na comunicação, risco de alarmes falsos e o fato de que o aplicativo suporta decisões, mas não substitui uma avaliação médica.

projectDetails.name: RotaSafra - DataLab
projectDetails.summary:
RotaSafra is an intelligent agricultural decision-support platform developed by the DataLab Academic League for the NASA Space Apps Challenge. Our project aims to help Brazilian farmers make smarter, more sustainable planting decisions by combining NASA Earth observation data, climate information, soil conditions, and crop history.

The platform uses a seven-component analytical architecture to evaluate climate, soil health, water availability, agricultural risk zoning (ZARC), crop rotation strategies, and environmental risks. Through scenario simulation and a scoring system, RotaSafra ranks potential crops based on their suitability for each farm, providing transparent recommendations, risk assessments, and insights aligned with farmers' production goals.

By transforming complex environmental data into accessible and actionable insights, RotaSafra addresses challenges such as climate change, soil degradation, and water scarcity. Our mission is to empower farmers with data-driven technology, promoting agricultural productivity, environmental sustainability, and long-term resilience.
projectDetails.details:
🌱 RotaSafra — Project Details

RotaSafra is an intelligent agricultural decision-support platform developed by the DataLab Academic League at the Federal University of Uberlândia (UFU), Brazil, for the NASA Space Apps Challenge. Our mission is to transform NASA Earth observation data into practical, accessible, and scientifically informed crop rotation recommendations.

Explore RotaSafra in action through our demonstration videos, showcasing the platform's interface and features across web and mobile devices.

  • 🖥️ Web Version — Presentation: Watch on YouTube
  • 📱 Mobile Web Version — Presentation: Watch on YouTube
  • 💻 Explore Our GitHub Repository: RotaSafra — GitHub Repository

How Does It Work?

RotaSafra helps farmers decide what and when to plant by analyzing their geographical location, previous crops, soil conditions, environmental challenges, planting schedules, and production objectives.

The platform is designed around six independent analytical components, called Analysis Towers:

  1. Climate Analysis: Evaluates temperature, precipitation, historical weather patterns, and extreme climate events.
  2. Soil Analysis: Examines soil fertility, nutrient availability, compaction, and soil recovery potential.
  3. Water Analysis: Assesses soil moisture, water availability, drought risks, and crop water requirements.
  4. Agricultural Risk Zoning (ZARC): Evaluates planting suitability based on Brazil's official agricultural climate risk zoning guidelines.
  5. Crop Rotation Analysis: Examines previous crops, nutrient cycling, biological nitrogen fixation, pest management, and soil conservation.
  6. Eligibility Analysis: Considers regulatory restrictions, agricultural financing and insurance requirements.
  7. Extreme Risk Analysis: Contains the analysis of extreme weather risks.

Each component generates scores that are combined by a central evaluation system. Instead of relying on a single prediction, RotaSafra simulates different planting scenarios and ranks crops according to their suitability and the farmer's priorities.

The platform is designed to provide ranked recommendations, explanations, individual analysis scores, potential benefits, identified risks, and confidence indicators, allowing farmers to understand the reasoning behind each recommendation.

Technologies and Data Sources

RotaSafra's proposed architecture combines geospatial intelligence, environmental data analysis, scenario simulation, and computational scoring methods.

NASA Earth observation datasets are central to our approach, including:

  • NASA POWER: Climate and meteorological information.
  • SMAP: Soil moisture observations.
  • GPM: Precipitation measurements.
  • ECOSTRESS: Land surface temperature and thermal stress.
  • Landsat and MODIS: Vegetation monitoring and environmental changes.
  • GRACE/GRACE-FO: Water storage trends.

The platform also considers Brazilian agricultural information, particularly official ZARC guidelines, to connect environmental observations with local farming conditions.

Machine learning techniques may complement specific analytical components when suitable training and validation data are available.

What Makes RotaSafra Innovative?

Our main innovation is a flexible, explainable, and farmer-centered decision-support architecture.

Rather than recommending crops based solely on historical productivity, RotaSafra evaluates multiple environmental and agricultural dimensions simultaneously.

The system considers that different farmers have different priorities. While one farmer may focus on maximizing income, another may prioritize water conservation, soil restoration, nitrogen enrichment, or reducing climate-related risks.

By combining independent analytical components with scenario simulation, RotaSafra aims to provide personalized recommendations while making the factors behind each decision transparent.

Expected Benefits and Impact

RotaSafra aims to contribute to more productive, sustainable, and climate-resilient agriculture by:

  • Improving crop rotation and planting decisions.
  • Supporting soil conservation and nutrient management.
  • Promoting more efficient water resource utilization.
  • Reducing agricultural vulnerability to climate variability.
  • Helping farmers identify environmentally suitable planting opportunities.
  • Making complex satellite and agricultural information more accessible.
  • Supporting informed decisions for small, medium, and large agricultural producers.

Our team considered critical challenges such as climate change, regional environmental differences, soil degradation, water scarcity, agricultural risks, data reliability, and the need for interpretable recommendations.

RotaSafra does not seek to replace agricultural expertise. Instead, it aims to empower farmers and agricultural professionals with accessible, evidence-based insights.

Ultimately, our vision is to bridge the gap between space technology and everyday agricultural decision-making, helping build a more sustainable and resilient future for farming.

projectDetails.name: TerraTurn
projectDetails.summary: TerraTurn is a responsive web app, installable on a phone, that helps farmers decide what to plant after their current crop. The farmer draws the field boundary on a satellite map and enters the current crop and priorities. TerraTurn pulls NASA data for the field's centre (daily NASA POWER climate from 2005 to 2024, plus MODIS vegetation and evapotranspiration) and calculates, in code, the bare-soil months, the water deficit and the sowing windows. A language model then compares three crop rotations, the current one and two alternatives, and explains for each why it was suggested, the evidence with NASA numbers, the benefits, the risks and the uncertainty, with a plain-language recommendation. The model does no arithmetic: it only explains the engine's numbers and may only suggest crops from a table of 31 crops. TerraTurn answers the Field Shift challenge by turning hard-to-use satellite data into a practical decision, while showing its limits. It supports farmers and does not replace local agronomists.
projectDetails.details:
What it does and how it works

  1. The farmer outlines the property on a satellite map and enters the current crop, sowing month, soil, irrigation and priorities (10 options, such as soil health, saving water and protection against erosion), for a planning horizon of 1 to 24 months.
  2. The app pulls NASA data for the field's centre point: NASA POWER daily rain, temperature and soil moisture from 2005 to 2024 (about 50 km grid); MODIS MOD13Q1 vegetation (NDVI), 250 m, 2020-2024; and MODIS MOD16A2 evapotranspiration, 500 m, 2021-2024. Data loads in stages and is cached, so a second analysis of the same area is fast.
  3. A deterministic engine calculates the facts in code: bare-soil months (NDVI below 0.30), water balance (rain minus evapotranspiration), deficit months, start of the rains, dry spells, start of the season and the sowing windows of each crop.
  4. Claude Haiku 5.5 receives only those facts and the crops suitable for the area. It returns 3 rotations (the current one and two alternatives), 1 recommendation and a message to the farmer. A validator checks the calendar, the crops and that the answer cites the data's numbers, and sends errors back to the model up to 2 times.
  5. Each rotation comes with evidence, benefits, risks and an uncertainty level (low, medium or high), plus the notice "Validate with a local agronomist before deciding." Each indicator card shows its source and resolution, to make clear that a value from a 50 km grid is not a measurement of the field. A chat answers free questions using only the farm's data.
  6. You can try it now. The site opens in a demo without login, with 9 fictional farms and real NASA data in Brazil, Argentina and the USA.

Benefits

  • Turns satellite data that is hard to access into a planting decision in plain language, for people with no remote-sensing background.
  • Shows source, resolution and uncertainty in every result.
  • Costs about US$0.006 and 30 seconds per analysis, and about US$0.002 per chat question.

Intended impact

Help farmers plan rotations that keep the soil covered and use water better in a less stable climate, and bring a base of evidence to the conversation with agronomists. The app works for any coordinate. It does not predict yield, price or cost.

Tools

Front end: React 19, TypeScript, Vite, MapLibre, Leaflet, Three.js, Recharts. Back end: Python 3.12, FastAPI, SQLAlchemy, Pandas, NumPy, Shapely. PostgreSQL (Neon), Cloudflare Workers, Render. Claude Haiku 5.5 through the Anthropic API. Figma and the Inter font for design. Code: https://github.com/terra-turn-team/terraturn

How it is creative

We separate who calculates (the engine) from who explains (the model), and a validator checks every answer.

AI-first interface, with a no-signup demo built on real data.

Uncertainty and data gaps are shown to the farmer.

  • Factors we considered and limits
  • Built for rainfed farming. A farm marked as irrigated gets a warning.
  • NASA POWER has a ~50 km grid and was about 24% below the INMET station in Uberaba for rain (temperature r = 0.93). NDVI and evapotranspiration come from one pixel at the field's centre.
  • The crop table is an approximate reference (FAO ECOCROP, Embrapa/ZARC, FAO/USDA/MAFF crop calendars) with no agronomist review, because the team has no agronomist.
  • The data is historical. The app does not forecast and does not invent yield, price or dose.
  • Tests: 56 rotation analyses and 124 chat questions. The automatic evaluator flagged 52/56 and 123/124; after we separated the evaluator's false positives, 56/56 and 124/124. The suggested sowing month matched the SAGE crop calendar in 89% of cases (203/229). 31 back-end and 8 front-end automated tests pass.
  • Privacy: Argon2id password hashing, HttpOnly session cookie, per-user data isolation, data export and account deletion.
  • The first load can take up to about 50 seconds (free hosting).

Use of AI

In the product, Claude Haiku 5.5 writes the rotations, the recommendation and the chat answers, using only numbers calculated by the deterministic engine and the crop table. In development, we used Claude Code (Claude models) to integrate the engine into the API, write back-end and front-end code and tests, build the results screen, the demo, the mobile layout and the translations, configure deployment and draft the documentation. The team reviewed and approved the changes before merging. A second AI acted as an "agronomist reviewer" for the crop table. The engine's test batteries were run with Claude models. Early prototypes tested other models (OpenRouter).

projectDetails.name: Project Flipflop 34
projectDetails.summary: Earth System Trend Detective turns NASA Earth observations into an interactive, statistically audited investigation. Users compare variables and regions worldwide to learn what is changing, where, by how much, and whether it is significant. Robust trends, seasonality removal, AR(1)+FDR correction, extreme detection, guided maps and an explainable Scientific Bench make climate evidence accessible.
projectDetails.details:
Earth System Trend Detective is an interactive web platform created for the NASA Space Apps “Be an Earth System Trend Detective!” challenge. Its purpose is to transform decades of Earth observation data into understandable, reproducible, and statistically audited evidence. Instead of presenting isolated charts, the platform guides users through four central investigative questions: What is changing? Where is it changing? By how much? Is the observed signal statistically significant?

Why It Matters (Real-World Impact)

Climate time series are notoriously easy to misread: a single El Niño year can masquerade as a long-term trend, seasonal cycles distort naive comparisons, and straight-line regressions hide abrupt regime shifts. Earth System Trend Detective bridges the gap between raw satellite archives and trustworthy public decisions—helping science journalists avoid misleading claims about extreme events, educators and students explore teleconnections and agricultural drought interactively, and watershed or agricultural managers inspect heat–soil coupling and hydrological shifts without heavy computational infrastructure.

Guided Storytelling Before Free Exploration

Rather than dropping users into a blank map, the journey opens in an interactive 3D Blue Marble Story Hub that illustrates three classic statistical traps, introduces four investigation archetypes (Spatial Contrast, Local Cause & Effect, Cross-Teleconnection, and Univariate X-Ray), and offers four one-click investigations: Cerrado vs. Central Amazon soil moisture, Northern Minas Gerais heatwaves vs. soil drying (Same Location), Amazon solar radiation vs. Southern Brazil precipitation, and Arctic (Svalbard) vs. Tropical Atlantic warming. From there, an eight-step guided HUD tutorial transitions users smoothly into unrestricted global exploration.

Interactive Global Mapping & Grid Reconciliation

The interactive 2D Canvas map puts the entire globe in the user's hands through a clear, customizable workflow: first, users select variables X and Y from the available catalog; second, they choose the desired analysis time period; and third, they define two spatial regions (A and B) anywhere on Earth. Area selection is highly customizable—users can compose each region cell by cell with individual clicks, drag directly over the map, or drop 3×3 blocks, building connected footprints of up to 25 cells per area. A dedicated Same Location mode compares two distinct variables over the exact same physical area, and whenever chosen datasets use different native grids, the platform automatically reconciles coordinates across resolutions, including MERRA-2 (0.5° × 0.625°) and CERES (1° × 1°) grids. Trend markers, significance filters, hotspots, cartographic layers, and navigation controls further help users recognize spatial patterns worldwide without losing scientific context.

Explainable Scientific Bench

The Scientific Bench converts any map selection into a transparent, auditable diagnosis. Users can switch instantaneously between original monthly series, monthly climatological anomalies, and standardized Z-Scores (σ), toggle between Linear and Symlog scales, and inspect X–Y scatter plots alongside seasonality, trend trajectories, regional contrasts, extreme events, and the four final detective answers. Complete series and statistical metadata can be exported as structured JSON and CSV for independent verification and reuse.

Statistically Audited Engine

The statistical engine was engineered to prevent common pitfalls in environmental trend communication. Trend magnitude is estimated via robust Theil–Sen regression (with 95% confidence intervals) alongside ordinary least squares diagnostics. Temporal persistence is handled through AR(1) effective sample-size corrections and Hamed–Rao/Santer-style significance adjustments, while Benjamini–Hochberg False Discovery Rate (FDR) control adjusts q-values across spatial cells and multiple hypotheses. Nonlinear spline/GAM analysis detects acceleration and regime shifts, multivariate Mahalanobis distance (D_M > 2.5) flags extreme months without discarding signal, and scale-aware safeguards strictly forbid invalid percentage-change claims on interval variables such as temperature.

NASA & Multi-Source Data Architecture

The data architecture unifies five principal source families through a common contract and catalog: NASA POWER, NASA AppEEARS (MODIS), NASA Giovanni/GES DISC via CMR, Copernicus GloFAS via the Open-Meteo Flood API, and NOAA Climate Data Online. The catalog organizes seven environmental families spanning 42 backend operational variable codes and 43 user-facing UI entries across temperature, precipitation, atmospheric moisture, soil conditions, drought, river discharge, vegetation, radiation, clouds, wind, and ground stations—recording each variable's source, unit, native grid, temporal span, measurement scale, and operating mode. For fast global exploration, the frontend ships with 12 validated global NASA POWER trend grids (144 points each, 1981–2025), while live and credential-backed connectors fetch current and higher-resolution observations—backed by disk caching, missing-value sanitation, common-period alignment, and unit normalization.

Statistical Co-Pilot & Dynamic Discovery Engine

An optional Statistical Co-Pilot translates complex diagnostics into clear explanations, featuring a dedicated quick plain-language summary action as well as interactive Q&A. It integrates Google Gemini or OpenRouter when credentials are configured, while a deterministic fallback preserves core guidance without external generative AI. Constrained by seven inviolable scientific invariants and deterministic backend tools, the Co-Pilot cannot fabricate significance, alter computed statistics, or express invalid percentage changes. Complementing user-driven comparisons, a sub-50 ms dynamic discovery engine evaluates nonlinear regimes, CUSUM structural breaks, partial lagged teleconnections, physical attribution, and multivariate extremes—paired with a research pipeline using 5-block purged chronological cross-validation across five South American river basins, explicitly framing lagged associations as temporal evidence and candidate mechanisms rather than automatic proof of causality.

Architecture & Verification

Built with React, TypeScript, Vite, Mantine, Leaflet Canvas, and Plotly on the frontend over a modular Python statistical backend and REST API, the platform is backed by automated unit, contract, and Playwright end-to-end tests. Persistent sessions, responsive layouts, and transparent methodology make the platform accessible to students and citizens while preserving the provenance and rigor required by researchers.

Your challenge is to create a tool that can select variables measured by Earth science missions or produced by Earth science models, visualize how they change over time, and determine what is changing, where it is changing, how much it is changing, and if these changes are what scientists call “significant.”

projectDetails.name: Vigília — Explainable Health Monitoring for Astronauts
projectDetails.summary: Vigília is an offline web app that helps astronauts notice changes in their own health and know what to do, without depending on a live link to Earth. It follows the flow Collect → Interpret → Guide. Crew members log seven indicators: resting heart rate, heart rate variability, blood pressure, sleep, self-reported mood/stress/fatigue, body mass and exercise load. A deterministic rule engine compares each measurement with the astronaut's own pre-flight baseline, never with population ranges. It recognizes patterns across signals: short sleep, falling HRV and rising heart rate together become an "overload" alert. It also links exercise adherence to body-mass loss, without claiming causation. Every alert shows the formula, the numbers behind it, practical guidance, the NASA source, and when to contact the crew medical officer. Missing data is shown as "Not assessed", never as "Normal". The demo uses clearly labeled synthetic data in three scenarios. Vigília matters because on long missions, communication delays and limited medical resources mean the crew must detect problems early and act on their own.
projectDetails.details:
WHAT IT DOES

Vigília monitors astronaut health over a mission in three steps:

1. Collect: crew members log measurements (manual entry with validation, plus a 1–5 self-report of mood, stress and fatigue). Each value carries its origin: Synthetic, Measured or Estimated.

2. Interpret: a pure, deterministic rule engine compares each value with the astronaut's individual pre-flight baseline (7 days). Rules: resting HR z-score, HRV drop, blood-pressure drift, accumulated sleep deficit, self-report decline, body-mass loss and exercise adherence. A composite rule detects overload (sleep ↓, HRV ↓, HR ↑ together). An association rule links body-mass loss with low exercise adherence over 21 days, using the language of possibility, never causation. Combined with a blood-pressure deviation, it escalates to the crew medical officer.

3. Guide: every alert shows its title, explanation, the exact arithmetic, the numeric evidence (current × baseline × deviation), preventive guidance, the scientific source, and whether to escalate. The crew can log what they did ("Measurement repeated", "CMO contacted", "Action completed").

KEY FEATURES

- Explainable by design: no alert exists without a visible formula. Thresholds without a published source are labeled "Arbitrary threshold · subject to clinical validation".

- "No alert" is never shown as "normal": when data is missing, stale or the baseline is still forming, the signal is shown as "Not assessed" with the reason.

- Each indicator is mapped to a NASA HRP spaceflight hazard and comes with microgravity-adapted measurement instructions (for example, blood pressure with the body restrained, mass measured by linear acceleration).

- Mission track: replay any mission day and see exactly when each pattern emerged.

- Crew registration: up to 8 members with role on board; each member's data, baseline and actions stay separate.

- Works offline (service worker, local storage, no backend), because an app for astronauts must work without Earth.

- Bilingual interface (English / Portuguese), light and dark themes, responsive, keyboard and screen-reader friendly; status is never conveyed by color alone.

DEMO SCENARIOS (synthetic data, 120 days each)

1. Nominal: stays "Normal" on all 113 mission days, with zero false positives.

2. Gradual degradation: the overload alert fires on day 102.

3. Critical with countermeasure: low exercise adherence, body-mass loss and blood-pressure drift escalate to the crew medical officer on day 111.

All scenarios are checked by 76 automated tests.

TOOLS AND TECHNOLOGIES

TypeScript, React 18, Vite, Recharts, Vitest; rule engine in plain TypeScript with no dependencies; service worker for offline use; static deployment on Vercel. Open source under Apache-2.0.

CREATIVITY AND DESIGN CHOICES

Instead of a dashboard of vital signs, Vigília reads patterns across signals and tells the astronaut what to do. It deliberately associates rather than models, keeps AI out of the decision path so every alert stays auditable, and is honest about its limits.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

Communication delay and offline operation; crew fatigue and limited time; individual baselines instead of clinical cutoffs; false-alarm prevention (SD floors, consecutive-day rules); data honesty (synthetic data labeled everywhere); privacy (nicknames only, data stays on the device); and the limits of a non-diagnostic tool.

LIMITATIONS AND FUTURE WORK

Thresholds need clinical validation; there is no real astronaut telemetry; there is no login or access control. Next steps: radiation dosimetry as mission context, SANS screening, bone markers, validation with aerospace medical teams, and adaptation for remote environments on Earth (Antarctic bases, offshore platforms).

projectDetails.name: Project Forsaken Elite
projectDetails.summary: Solar Atlas is an interactive web platform turning NASA's hardware left on the Moon, Mars, and deep space into visual stories, connecting engineering design to science to inspire STEM students.
projectDetails.details:
What does it do and how does it work? Solar Atlas functions as an interactive guide and digital museum of the Solar System dedicated to NASA's historical space artifacts—equipment that fulfilled its missions on the lunar and Martian surfaces, or probes that continue traveling through deep space.

Upon accessing the application, users navigate through different destinations (the Moon, Mars, and Deep Space) and historical eras to explore each piece of equipment in detail:

Guided Narrative (Storytelling): Instead of presenting dry technical spec sheets, each artifact (such as the Apollo Lunar Modules, the Lunar Roving Vehicle, the Surveyor and Viking probes, or the Sojourner, Spirit, Opportunity, and InSight rovers) is given an engaging narrative that explains why it was built, the extreme challenges it faced, how it operated, and its current status.

Bridge Between Engineering and Science: The platform breaks down complex systems—such as heat shields, radioisotope thermoelectric generators (RTGs), seismometers, and spectral cameras—into educational and visual explanations, demonstrating how each piece of hardware enabled fundamental discoveries (such as confirming past water on Mars or revealing the internal structure of the Moon).

Visual Exploration and 3D Models: It integrates visual references and official NASA 3D resources so students can inspect the anatomy of the spacecraft and understand their scale and functionality.

What benefits does it bring and what is the intended impact?

Democratization of Space Science: It removes the barrier of dense technical reports and academic textbooks, delivering rigorous scientific content in clear, exciting, and jargon-free language for school-age youth and casual enthusiasts.

Pedagogical Support for Educators (STEM): It provides science, physics, and technology teachers with a ready-to-use interactive classroom tool, making it easier to teach concepts of aerospace engineering, robotics, and astronomy.

Emotional Connection and Inspiration: By presenting inactive equipment not as "discarded scrap," but as robotic pioneers and archaeological heritage of humanity, the project sparks scientific curiosity and encourages young people to pursue careers in science, technology, engineering, and mathematics (STEM).

Tools, programming languages, hardware, and software used

Artificial Intelligence and Prototyping: Google AI Studio and Gemini API for structuring the application's architecture, curating educational content, and adapting technical engineering language into educational storytelling tailored for students.

Front-End Development: React, TypeScript, JavaScript (ES6+), HTML5, and Tailwind CSS / CSS3 to build a fast, responsive Single-Page Application (SPA) with an immersive aesthetic inspired by space telemetry interfaces.

Design, Icons, and Typography: Google Fonts and Lucide Icons to ensure high readability, accessible contrast, and an intuitive visual hierarchy.

Infrastructure and Deployment: Cloud hosting via Google AI Studio Apps (https://atlas-solar.ai.studio/), enabling instant browser access across computers, tablets, and smartphones with no installation required.

How is the project creative? The project subverts the common perception of "abandoned equipment" by treating every inactive probe, lander, and rover as a historical character and a living monument to human engineering. Instead of listing dates and specifications in a static table, the Solar Hardware Atlas creates a space exploration experience where students uncover the "invisible legacy" of each machine—showing that a silent rover covered in Martian dust still tells the story of how we learned to navigate another world.

What factors did the team consider?

Age and Language Appropriateness: We calibrated the depth of the text to captivate school-age students and beginners while maintaining 100% fidelity to historical facts and real NASA mission data.

Accessibility and Performance: We designed a lightweight, intuitive, and responsive web interface, ensuring that schools or users with modest internet connections and devices can navigate the experience smoothly without lag.

Balance Between Scope and Depth: We selected iconic missions distributed across the Moon, Mars, and Deep Space to illustrate both the technological evolution since the 1960s and the diverse functions of space hardware (landing, mobility, sample collection, communication, and seismic measurement).

Versão em Português

O que ele faz e como funciona?

O Atlas Solar funciona como um guia interativo e museu digital do Sistema Solar dedicado aos artefatos espaciais históricos da NASA — equipamentos que cumpriram suas missões na superfície lunar e marciana ou sondas que seguem viajando pelo espaço profundo.

Ao acessar a aplicação o usuário navega por diferentes destinos (Lua, Marte e Espaço Profundo) e épocas históricas para explorar cada equipamento em detalhes:

Narrativa Guiada (Storytelling): Em vez de apresentar fichas técnicas áridas, cada artefato (como os módulos lunares Apollo, o Lunar Roving Vehicle, as sondas Surveyor e Viking, ou os rovers Sojourner, Spirit, Opportunity e InSight) ganha uma narrativa envolvente que explica por que foi construído, os desafios extremos que enfrentou, como operava e seu estado atual.

Ponte entre Engenharia e Ciência: A plataforma decompõe sistemas complexos — como escudos térmicos, geradores termoelétricos de radioisótopos (RTGs), sismômetros e câmeras espectrais — em explicações didáticas e visuais, demonstrando como cada peça de hardware permitiu descobertas fundamentais (como a confirmação de água no passado de Marte ou a estrutura interna da Lua).

Exploração Visual e Modelos 3D: Integra referências visuais e recursos tridimensionais oficiais da NASA para que estudantes possam inspecionar a anatomia das espaçonaves e compreender sua escala e funcionamento.

Quais benefícios isso traz e qual é o impacto pretendido?

Democratização da Ciência Espacial: Elimina a barreira dos relatórios técnicos e livros acadêmicos densos, entregando conteúdo científico rigoroso em uma linguagem clara, empolgante e livre de jargões para jovens em idade escolar e entusiastas casuais.

Apoio Pedagógico para Educadores (STEM): Oferece a professores de ciências, física e tecnologia uma ferramenta interativa pronta para uso em sala de aula, facilitando o ensino de conceitos de engenharia aeroespacial, robótica e astronomia.

Conexão Emocional e Inspiração: Ao apresentar equipamentos inativos não como "sucata descartada", mas como pioneiros robóticos e patrimônios arqueológicos da humanidade, o projeto desperta curiosidade científica e incentiva jovens a seguirem carreiras nas áreas de ciência, tecnologia, engenharia e matemática.

Ferramentas, linguagens de programação, hardware e software utilizados:

Inteligência Artificial e Prototipação: Google AI Studio e Gemini API para estruturação arquitetural da aplicação, curadoria de conteúdo educativo e adaptação da linguagem técnica de engenharia para storytelling didático voltado ao público estudantil.

Desenvolvimento Front-End: React, TypeScript, JavaScript (ES6+), HTML5 e Tailwind CSS / CSS3 para construir uma Single-Page Application (SPA) responsiva, rápida e com estética imersiva inspirada em interfaces de telemetria espacial.

Design, Ícones e Tipografia: Google Fonts e Lucide Icons para garantir alta legibilidade, contraste acessível e hierarquia visual intuitiva.

Infraestrutura e Deploy: Hospedagem em nuvem via Google AI Studio Apps (https://atlas-solar.ai.studio/), permitindo acesso instantâneo via navegador em computadores, tablets e smartphones sem necessidade de instalação.

Como o projeto é criativo?

O projeto subverte a percepção comum de "equipamento abandonado" ao tratar cada sonda, lander e rover inativo como um personagem histórico e monumento vivo da engenharia humana. Em vez de listar datas e especificações em uma tabela estática, o Atlas do Hardware Solar cria uma experiência de exploração espacial onde o estudante descobre o "legado invisível" de cada máquina — mostrando que um rover silencioso coberto de poeira marciana ainda conta a história de como aprendemos a navegar em outro mundo.

Quais fatores a equipe considerou?

Adequação de Faixa Etária e Linguagem: Calibramos a profundidade do texto para cativar estudantes em idade escolar e iniciantes, mantendo 100% de fidelidade aos fatos históricos e dados reais das missões da NASA.

Acessibilidade e Desempenho: Projetamos uma interface web leve, intuitiva e responsiva, garantindo que escolas ou usuários com conexões e dispositivos modestos possam navegar pela experiência sem travamentos.

Equilíbrio entre Escopo e Profundidade: Selecionamos missões icônicas distribuídas entre a Lua, Marte e o Espaço Profundo para ilustrar tanto a evolução tecnológica desde os anos 1960 quanto a diversidade de funções do hardware espacial (pouso, locomoção, coleta de amostras, comunicação e medição sísmica).
