projectDetails.name: Future Foundation
projectDetails.summary:
Orbit is a health self-monitoring system that turns each astronaut into the first responder for their own health, even when the nearest doctor is 20 light-minutes away.

On long missions to the Moon and Mars, delays and blackouts make real-time medical support impossible, while risks like bone loss, vision changes (SANS), radiation, and isolation develop slowly and silently. Astronauts can take measurements but are not doctors, so they need help interpreting them.

Orbit combines a 2-minute daily check-in, wearable data (heart rate, SpO2, eye attention) and radiation readings. Each value is compared with the astronaut's own baseline and, where they exist, official NASA limits, then shown on a clickable body map with a color, an icon and a word for every state. Every alert explains its rule, its evidence and the recommended action, in supportive language rather than diagnosis.

The prototype runs offline with simulated data and includes a crew view and an offline assistant. Next step: syncing compact reports to flight surgeons when a communication window opens.
projectDetails.details:
WHAT IT DOES / HOW IT WORKS

Orbit is a health self-monitoring system that helps astronauts assess and act on their own health during long missions, even without contact with Earth.

1. Collect: Orbit Glasses (concept) use EEG and EOG sensors to detect fatigue, stress and inattention, and deliver alerts through bone conduction so the crew can still hear their surroundings. The system also tracks heart rate, radiation dose and blood oxygen, plus a short daily check-in for hydration, fatigue, appetite and blood tests.

2. Understand: a 3D Digital Twin shows each body system color-coded green (nominal), yellow (monitor) or red (act), inspired by the radiation thresholds NASA used on Artemis II. Trend charts show how each indicator changes over time.

3. Act: each alert comes with one clear action. An AI assistant guides triage, and compact reports are sent to flight surgeons when a signal is available.

Other features: gamification, crew view and a radiation tracker.

BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT

Mars is up to 4 - 22 minutes away by message, with up to two - three weeks of no contact during solar conjunction. Orbit gives astronauts medical autonomy, detecting silent conditions like bone loss, cardiovascular changes and vision problems early. On Earth, it can support remote communities, polar stations, aircrews, elderly people living alone and disaster zones.

CREATIVITY

- A wearable that monitors the brain and eyes while keeping hearing free.

- Every alert is linked to one of NASA's 17 official spaceflight risks.

- A color system based on a real NASA protocol.

- Designed to work offline and sync with Earth when possible.

TOOLS AND TECHNOLOGIES

React, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, with support from Lovable, Claude Code, Traycer, Claude and ChatGPT. The demo uses synthetic mission data, and the Orbit Glasses are a hardware concept.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

Communication delays, astronauts not being doctors, underreported symptoms, accessibility (color, icon and text), and safety: Orbit supports decisions but does not diagnose, and flight surgeons stay in the loop.

projectDetails.name: Happy Farmers
projectDetails.summary:
Happy Farmers is a web-based decision-support tool that helps farmers in Minas Gerais, Brazil, choose their next crop rotation under a changing climate. The farmer draws a field on a satellite map, adds what was planted before, sets priorities for water, soil and income, and confirms the soil texture. The tool returns the three best rotations for today's climate next to the current rotation, each with its rank in the climate projected for around 2060.

The engine runs on NASA POWER (climate, 2005–2024), NASA NEX-GDDP-CMIP6 (three climate models), MODIS (vegetation), SRTM (terrain) and GLDAS (soil texture). Brazilian sources (INMET, IBGE, Conab, CEPEA, ZARC and Embrapa) add ground measurements, yields, prices and local farming rules. Its rules are transparent: every number on screen can be explained, each rotation lists benefits, risks and information gaps, and close scores are flagged as a technical tie.

Climate conditions keep shifting, and the ranking shifts with them: around 2060, rotations with beans and cotton fall behind, and in a dry year the usual soybean and maize rotation loses 27% of its revenue. Happy Farmers turns open NASA data into a decision farmers can discuss with their agronomist before planting.
projectDetails.details:
Happy Farmers' Project Solution

Happy Farmers is a web-based decision-support tool for crop rotation in the Brazilian Cerrado. A farmer draws a field on a satellite map, sets priorities and receives the three best rotations for today's climate, next to the rotation already in use. Each one shows how it ranks in the climate projected for around 2060. This first version covers fields in Minas Gerais, Brazil.

How Does Our Solution Work

1. Define the field. The farmer draws the boundary on satellite imagery or imports a GeoJSON file. The tool calculates the area and locates the field.

2. Add the crop history (optional). The most recent crops become the current rotation, which stays on screen as the reference for comparison.

3. Plan the next planting. The farmer chooses the month the field becomes available and whether to plan one or two crops.

4. Set priorities and soil. The farmer weights water, soil and income. The tool suggests a soil texture from NASA GLDAS, and the farmer confirms or changes it. Texture sets how much water the soil holds.

5. Get the climate for that exact spot. The tool fetches 20 years of daily NASA POWER data for the field's location and applies the change projected by three NASA NEX-GDDP-CMIP6 climate models (SSP2-4.5). The result represents the climate of around 2060.

6. Simulate every rotation. For 10 crops grown in the region, the engine simulates each sequence of one or two crops day by day in its planting window: crop water demand, soil water balance, temperature and rainfall fit, heat stress during flowering, and sequence rules (crop repetition, shared pests and diseases, nitrogen credit after a green manure).

7. Compare. Up to three rotations with the highest scores appear as cards. Each card shows today's score, the rank around 2060 and the range of that rank across the three climate models, with its benefits, risks and information gaps. A monthly calendar shows planting, harvest, water deficit and days of bare soil. Scores less than two points apart are flagged as a technical tie.

8. Explore. What-if sliders test less rain or more heat. At the demo field, a real dry year (2020/21) is a third scenario. An optional AI chat explains the numbers on screen; it never produces them.

What the Data Shows: Our Demo Field

Our demo field is a 219-hectare farm in the Triângulo Mineiro region of Minas Gerais.

Heat. Days above 35 °C rise from 34 per year today to about 70 per year around 2060. The three climate models agree on warming: +1.3 to +2.3 °C in the average daily maximum.

A technical tie at the top. With the field available in October, soybean followed by sunn hemp (78.2), soybean followed by maize (77.9) and soybean followed by sorghum (76.5) score within two points of each other. The tool flags the tie instead of declaring a winner.

Heat reshuffles the ranking. With the field available in February, common bean followed by soybean falls from 4th to 9th place around 2060: hot days during flowering cut the bean's heat fit from 77 to 45 out of 100. Maize followed by cotton falls from 8th to 17th.

A dry year. In the real dry season of 2020/21 (813 mm of rain, against an average of 1,236 mm), soybean followed by maize loses 27% of its revenue, from R$ 13,003 to R$ 9,438 per hectare, and drops from 2nd to 4th place.

Satellite plus ground. A weather station 40 km away (INMET A520) records nights 1.2 to 2.5 °C colder than the NASA POWER estimate. The tool applies this correction near the station and shows it to the farmer.

Bare soil. Ten years of MODIS vegetation data show signs of bare soil or crop residue in August (50% of years) and September (60% of years).

Benefits

Farmers compare rotations on water, soil and income before planting, with their own priorities, in plain language and with a glossary of scientific terms.

Agronomists get a transparent starting point: every score comes from documented rules, and each rotation lists the risks and the data that need local validation.

Communities gain access to climate projections that rarely reach the field in a usable form.


Our Goal

Our goal is to turn open NASA data into a decision farmers can discuss with their agronomist before planting. The tool supports local knowledge and does not replace it.

We are open about its limits. This version covers Minas Gerais, and the planting calendar comes from one region of the state. Revenue is gross, before production costs. Scores less than two points apart are a tie. The projected change in rainfall is not statistically significant: the three models agree on warming but disagree on rain. Vegetation history, slope, the dry year and the range across climate models are available only for the demo field. Some crop values are provisional and are flagged on screen.

Datasets we considered and left out. SMAP soil moisture (9 to 36 km, top 5 cm) is the natural next check for our modelled soil water. GPM IMERG would improve rainfall extremes. ECOSTRESS and Landsat would feed a map of zones inside the field, which we did not build.

Next steps: check the modelled soil water against SMAP, bring the engine's daily mode to the screen (frost days and extreme rain are already counted), add planting calendars for other regions and include production costs.


Tools and Technologies Used

Coding languages: Python (scoring engine, data pipeline and API), Rust compiled to WebAssembly (interface) and JavaScript (map and browser integration).

Frameworks and libraries: FastAPI, pandas, xarray, Rune and rune-kit, Leaflet and Leaflet-Geoman, Vite.

Infrastructure: Docker, Railway, GitHub Actions running automated tests on every change (178 engine tests).

Scoring engine: rules and arithmetic only, with no machine learning, so every number can be traced back to its source.

AI: an optional chat uses a large language model (Anthropic Claude) only to explain the engine's results.

projectDetails.name: Project Harmonia
projectDetails.summary:
Harmonia is a web app that turns NASA satellite images of Earth into music, so people can hear what they cannot see.

It loads true-colour imagery from NASA’s MODIS and VIIRS instruments through NASA GIBS, then divides each image into a grid of squares. Each square becomes a chord, following simple rules: brighter areas play higher notes, and mostly white areas such as clouds and ice play the highest; warm colours give major chords and cold colours minor chords; similar colours sound harmonic and mixed colours clash; and a square’s position sets whether the sound comes from the left or the right. People explore with a mouse, the arrow keys or a screen reader, or press Play to hear the whole image. A piano and meters show what is being played, and the page works in English and Portuguese.

The Earth Jukebox challenge asks for Earth science that is multisensory and accessible. 
Our project works as a new way to see images, works mixing music theory and color aspects of the image to create a sound.
We reached the objective of the challenge because we have implemented a way to translate sight into sound and this is important because the work can be used by blind people, and has much potential to expand.

Harmonia's source code, tests and documentation were written with Claude Code directed by our team. Our team defined the concept and the image-to-sound rules, chose the NASA images and tested the result. All images are real NASA satellite imagery

We propose a system through which children, students, schools, and universities can build their own robotic exploration vehicles using Arduino or other microcontrollers, equipped with sensors to collect environmental and terrain data, including temperature, atmospheric pressure, humidity, terrain inclination, elevation, and surface characteristics.

projectDetails.details:
Planetary Explorers – A Collaborative Platform for Extraterrestrial Terrain Analog Mapping and Space Exploration Simulation

What does the project do and how does it work?

Our project was conceived around a fundamental question: how can we bring society closer to space exploration while contributing to the challenges of planning and preparing future missions to the Moon and Mars?

We propose the development of an open, collaborative technological platform that integrates robotics, citizen science, STEM education, environmental sensing, and planetary exploration.

The concept is to enable children, students, schools, universities, and technology enthusiasts to build their own robotic exploration vehicles using a DIY (Do It Yourself) approach, based on Arduino or other compatible microcontroller platforms.

These vehicles will be equipped with environmental and terrain-monitoring sensors capable of collecting multiple parameters, including temperature, atmospheric pressure, relative humidity, wind speed, terrain inclination, elevation, surface morphology, and soil characteristics such as sand, rocks, sandstone, and other geological formations.

Once collected, the measurements will be transmitted to a centralized digital platform, where the information will be processed, organized, and compared against scientific and geospatial datasets made available by NASA concerning the surfaces of Mars and the Moon.

Through geospatial analysis and multi-parameter similarity assessment, the platform will identify terrestrial environments that exhibit comparable physical and morphological characteristics to selected extraterrestrial locations.

The results will be displayed through interactive maps, allowing users to visualize potential terrestrial analog sites and understand their similarities to specific regions of Mars and the Moon.

For example, a student operating a robotic vehicle across a sandy environment in Brazil could discover that the terrain presents morphological characteristics comparable to a particular region of Mars or the lunar surface.

What benefits does the project provide?

The primary benefit is democratizing access to space science, robotics, and scientific research.

Through an accessible and modular architecture, participants can independently build robotic vehicles, develop embedded systems, program microcontrollers, integrate environmental sensors, and contribute to a collaborative scientific data network.

Beyond its educational value, the platform aims to establish a crowdsourced database of terrestrial environments that may serve as analogs for extraterrestrial terrain conditions.

By gathering measurements from geographically diverse locations and contrasting environmental conditions, the project will expand the availability of field data for comparative planetary science and terrestrial analog research.

What is the intended impact?

Our vision is to transform the public from passive observers of space exploration into active contributors to scientific discovery.

Imagine students collecting environmental and terrain data across the sand dunes of São Luís, Brazil, semi-arid regions, the Atacama Desert in Chile, frozen environments in Canada, and other extreme terrestrial landscapes.

Each participant can contribute measurements from their local environment, helping build an international network for terrestrial terrain characterization.

These datasets could support researchers, educational institutions, and space exploration organizations in identifying and evaluating potential terrestrial analog environments for planetary research, technology testing, and mission simulation.

The project also seeks to strengthen global STEM education by making planetary science accessible through hands-on experimentation.

Our goal is to allow children and young people to experience what it means to be scientists, engineers, and planetary explorers, demonstrating that meaningful contributions to space exploration can begin right here on Earth.

What tools and technologies were used?

The project integrates hardware, embedded software, robotics, environmental instrumentation, and geospatial data analysis.

The main technologies include:

- Arduino and other compatible microcontrollers for robotic vehicle control.

- Environmental sensors for temperature, atmospheric pressure, relative humidity, and wind measurements.

- Inclinometers, altitude sensors, and terrain-monitoring instruments.

- Electric motors, electronic components, and mechanical structures for robotic mobility.

- C programming language for embedded systems development.

- Code::Blocks and Visual Studio Code as software development environments.

- A web-based platform for data transmission, processing, storage, analysis, and visualization.

- NASA scientific datasets, planetary maps, and geospatial resources for comparative terrain analysis.

The system architecture is designed to support different microcontroller platforms, allowing flexibility, modularity, scalability, and broader community participation.

What makes the project creative and innovative?

The most innovative aspect is the integration of DIY robotics, citizen science, and planetary terrain analog research into a single collaborative ecosystem.

Traditionally, scientific information about Mars and the Moon is obtained through specialized space missions, orbital instruments, robotic landers, and scientific exploration systems.

Our proposal introduces a complementary approach: a distributed terrestrial exploration network in which ordinary people can build their own robotic vehicles, collect environmental measurements, and contribute to a shared database of terrestrial analog environments.

We are not simply teaching people how to build robots. We are creating an opportunity for participants to investigate how terrestrial environments compare with the landscapes of other planetary bodies.

The project combines open-source hardware, accessible programming, environmental data acquisition, collaborative scientific participation, and planetary geospatial analysis.

It transforms the concept of learning through robotics into an active contribution to the broader field of space exploration.

What factors did the team consider?

Throughout the development process, our team considered several fundamental aspects:

- Financial accessibility and ease of replication of robotic vehicles.

- Compatibility with different microcontrollers, sensors, and hardware architectures.

- Measurement reliability, calibration, and data standardization.

- Geographic and environmental diversity of participating locations.

- Safety and ease of use for children, students, and educational institutions.

- Integration with NASA scientific and geospatial datasets.

- Platform scalability and international participation.

- Potential applications in scientific research, comparative terrain analysis, and planetary mission simulations.

Our vision for the future

We envision a global platform where thousands of people, across different countries and environments, can build their own planetary exploration vehicles and contribute to an international network for terrestrial analog characterization.

Every robotic vehicle becomes a learning instrument. Every student becomes a potential contributor to scientific discovery. Every dataset becomes an opportunity to better understand the environments beyond our planet.

Our mission is to transform human curiosity into technology, education into science, and terrestrial exploration into a bridge toward the exploration of space.

projectDetails.name: Kultive IoT: NASA Remote Sensing Soil Telemetry Data Fusion
projectDetails.summary:
Kultive IoT
Kultive IoT is a hybrid agricultural monitoring system that bridges macro-level space technology with micro-level ground telemetry.

What We Developed
We built low-cost field stations using ESP32 microcontrollers to measure localized soil moisture and stream real-time telemetry via MQTT. On the macro layer, our system automatically ingests root-zone soil moisture (0–100 cm) from the NASA SMAP L4 satellite (NASA/SMAP/SPL4SMGP/008) and precipitation data from NASA GPM IMERG via Google Earth Engine. A FastAPI/Python backend calibrates orbital satellite estimates against physical ground readings using linear regression to eliminate spatial bias[1], feeding a Flutter mobile application featuring interactive maps, dynamic marker color changes, and automated drought push notifications[1].

How It Addresses the Challenge
It overcomes the fundamental trade-off between coarse-resolution regional satellite maps (~9 km) and isolated ground-sensor point readings by unifying spaceborne climate context with field-level precision.

Why It Is Important
It transforms complex NASA Earth observation data into direct, real-time irrigation decisions in the palm of the farmer's hand—optimizing water consumption, preventing crop failure, and fostering agricultural sustainability
projectDetails.details:
🎯 Project Details

1. What does it do or how does it work?

Kultive IoT is a hybrid agricultural intelligence and precision irrigation solution that performs data fusion across two complementary layers:

  • Orbital Layer (Macro): Automatically retrieves root-zone soil moisture (0 to 100 cm) from the NASA SMAP Level-4 satellite (NASA/SMAP/SPL4SMGP/008) and accumulated precipitation from NASA GPM IMERG via Google Earth Engine.
  • Ground Layer (Micro): Deploys low-cost field stations based on ESP32 microcontrollers with capacitive moisture sensors installed at root depth, transmitting real-time telemetry via MQTT.
  • Data Fusion & Linear Regression Calibration: Because satellite observations cover a broad spatial resolution (~9 km to 11 km) while physical sensors measure specific points in the field, a FastAPI/Python backend cross-references historical timelines and applies linear regression (Linear Scaling). The algorithm calculates slope (\(m\)) and additive offset (\(c\)) to eliminate spatial bias and calibrate satellite estimates according to local soil physics.
  • Interface & Alerts: The calibrated data is delivered to a Flutter mobile application, displaying crop fields on interactive maps with dynamic color-coded markers and triggering local push notifications if soil moisture drops below critical levels (<20%).

2. What benefits does it have?

  • Resolves the Scale Discrepancy (Macro + Micro): Overcomes both the coarse detail of standalone satellite imagery (~9 km) and the lack of regional climatological context in standalone ground sensors.
  • High In-Soil Durability: Uses capacitive sensors to eliminate the electrolytic corrosion typical of resistive sensors, significantly extending field hardware lifespan.
  • Real-Time Critical Alerts: Instant visual and audio notifications alert farmers the moment a field enters critical drought stress (<20%).
  • Intuitive Cartographic Interface: Automatic color transitions for map markers (green/blue for adequate moisture, red for drought warning).
  • Ultra-Low Cost: Enables building each field node for an estimated hardware cost between R$ 80.00 and R$ 140.00 (~$15–$25 USD), taking advantage of completely free NASA Earth observation APIs.

3. What is the intended impact of the project?

  • Optimized Water Resource Management: Precise scheduling of irrigation pump activation, avoiding water waste when deeper root zones still retain sufficient moisture.
  • Risk Mitigation & Food Security: Protects sensitive crops (such as coffee plantations in Triângulo Mineiro, Brazil) against severe yield losses caused by flash droughts.
  • Democratizing Space Technology: Translates complex NASA Earth observation data into simple, actionable farm management decisions in the palm of the farmer's hand.

4. What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use?

  • Spatial Data & Cloud: NASA SMAP L4 (NASA/SMAP/SPL4SMGP/008), NASA GPM IMERG, and Google Earth Engine API.
  • Hardware & IoT: ESP32 DevKit V1 microcontroller (Dual-Core, Wi-Fi/Bluetooth), Capacitive Soil Moisture Sensor V1.2, 5V 1-Channel Relay Module (optoisolated), and 5V Submersible Mini Water Pump.
  • Protocols & Connectivity: MQTT Protocol (PubSubClient in C++ and mqtt_client in Dart) with Mosquitto/HiveMQ broker.
  • Backend & Data Science: Python 3.11, FastAPI, Pandas, NumPy, and SQLite.
  • Frontend Mobile & Web: Flutter, flutter_map (Leaflet.js / ESRI World Imagery), flutter_local_notifications, and a responsive HTML5/CSS3/JavaScript web mockup.
  • Hardware Simulation: Wokwi simulator for virtual circuit testing of the ESP32 and sensors.

5. How is your project creative?

  • Calibrated Spaceborne-Ground Fusion: Mathematical creativity in using local field readings as point "ground truth" to correct the radiometric bias of satellite imagery through linear scaling.
  • Dynamic Map Markers: Real-time visual UI transitions on smartphone maps, dynamically altering pin color and pulse animations based on incoming MQTT payload states.
  • Hybrid Simulation & Prototyping: A fully functional prototype pipeline integrating the Wokwi hardware simulator connected to live MQTT brokers and mobile application mockups during development.

6. What factors did your team consider?

  • Depth & Scale Differences: The team accounted for the distinction between surface moisture (0–5 cm) and root-zone moisture (0–100 cm), choosing SMAP's Level-4 product to align with root-depth ground sensors.
  • Farmer Financial Feasibility: Focused on affordable, readily available hardware components in local markets paired with zero-cost cloud infrastructure.
  • Field Operational Robustness: Selected corrosion-resistant capacitive sensors and weatherproof IP65 enclosures powered by rechargeable battery/solar setups to withstand farm environments.
  • User Experience (UX): Simple map interface supporting quick status visualization and direct push alerts without requiring complex user setup.

Furthermore, in each mission, children perform activities to keep the space station operational, such as generating electricity using solar panels, monitoring crew health, investigating soil composition, treating water, and experimenting with different cultivation methods. Its design was inspired by the visual style of the game Stardew Valley, recreating regions of the planet Mars, specifically the Arcadia Planitia region. Interaction with the game encourages scientific, critical, and technological thinking, inspiring new generations of astronauts and scientists.

MARS ADVENTURES: EDUCATIONAL SIMULATOR FOR SCIENTIFIC PRACTICES AND SPACE SURVIVAL

This project aims to develop Mars Adventure, an educational digital game that combines adventure, survival and science, challenging players to remain on Mars by completing missions inspired by astronauts' activities and the obstacles involved in space exploration. Throughout the experience, activities will be developed related to the installation of solar panels, monitoring the astronaut's health, geological investigation, water identification and treatment, growing food in greenhouses, and protection against Martian environmental phenomena.

As a learning aid, the game features Capi, a capybara who acts as a tutor and virtual assistant, guiding the player through missions, explaining scientific concepts, and helping interpret the information presented. The choice of the capybara is related to its popularity and recognition as a symbol of cultural identification among young Brazilians, as well as contributing to making the experience more welcoming and accessible. In addition, the game will include a logbook system for recording events, observations and results of experiments conducted during the expedition.

The main benefit of the proposal is to bring scientific knowledge closer to the students' reality through a playful and interactive experience. In this sense, it seeks to stimulate curiosity, logical reasoning, problem-solving, and scientific thinking, as well as broaden understanding of the importance of space research.

Regarding technological development, the languages ​​JavaScript, TypeScript, HTML, and CSS were used, in addition to tools such as Git and GitHub, intended for source code management and versioning, and artificial intelligence platforms such as ChatGPT, Gemini, and Claude, employed as resources to support programming and content creation. Antigravity and Cursor were also used, which assisted in the development of functionalities and the structuring of the game. The integration of these resources enabled the construction of the interfaces, interactive systems, and mechanics necessary for the proposed experience.

The originality of Mars Adventure lies in its integration of space survival, scientific investigation, and challenge-based learning. During development, aspects such as the scientific methodology for data collection in missions, age-appropriate language, information accessibility, challenge progression, and gameplay were also considered, aiming to transform complex scientific concepts into understandable and meaningful activities.

In light of the above, it can be concluded that Mars Adventure presents a proposal for integrating two axes, entertainment and education, using space exploration as a means for constructing scientific knowledge. Its application may contribute to sparking students' interest in science and technology, while simultaneously stimulating skills related to investigation, autonomy, and problem-solving. In this way, the project highlights the potential of digital games as tools to support learning and scientific dissemination.

projectDetails.name: Mars Academy
projectDetails.summary:
Mars Academy is an educational and interactive game aimed at children, in which the player takes on the role of an astronaut and must survive for ten days on Mars after Earth collapses.
The game addresses the challenge of survival on the Red Planet by placing the child at the center of decision-making. During the mission, they must manage six vital indicators (oxygen, water, food, energy, radiation, and health) while exploring the environment, completing nighttime tasks to collect items, and facing time-limited emergencies. All of this is integrated with educational explanations and real space phenomena, using official NASA sources and solar activity data from the NASA DONKI API.
This project is important because it teaches children to think critically, manage scarce resources, and understand the consequences of their own choices. In addition to sparking interest in science and space exploration in a fun way, the story reinforces an essential message about the importance of caring for and preserving planet Earth by understanding the difficulties we would face on another planet.
projectDetails.details:
Mars Academy is an educational game of survival, decision-making, and minigames aimed at children aged 7 to 12, also designed for use by teachers in the classroom. The application runs directly in the browser on computers, tablets, and smartphones, with each playthrough lasting an estimated 10 to 20 minutes.

Play the game online here: https://mars-academy.lovable.app/

The narrative takes place in the year 2045, in a scenario where Earth faces crises of environmental degradation, climate change, and resource scarcity. To address this reality, NASA creates Project New Horizon and sends four astronauts to Mars on a ten-day expedition. Shortly after landing, communication with Earth begins to fail, meaning the support team can only arrive on the tenth day. The player takes on the role of Maya — a specialist in astronomy and natural sciences — or Milo — focused on technology, robotics, and exploration — young astronauts-in-training participating in the mission through a NASA simulation. Throughout the journey, the team is accompanied by three specialists: Andreas, an aerospace engineer responsible for energy, equipment, and life support; Laika, a biologist and astrobiologist in charge of water, soil, climate, and cultivation; and Lina, a space physician focused on health, nutrition, and radiation.

The gameplay is divided into daytime and nighttime periods. During the day, one of the specialists presents a real Martian problem, such as dust storms, water scarcity, oxygen failures, excess carbon dioxide, among others. The player has three action alternatives, none of which are perfect; protecting a specific resource always comes at the cost of another, requiring choices based on logic and consequences that are followed by scientific explanations. Survival is monitored by six indicators that start at 70: oxygen, water, food, energy, radiation, and health. Of these, radiation never decreases, so decisions aim solely to avoid adding risk levels. At night, the player explores the base and can complete up to three of nine optional minigames, such as reconnecting circuits, restarting the oxygen generator, and cleaning solar panels. Each minigame shares real NASA trivia, and any failures result only in the loss of the reward. Additionally, on random nights, surprise emergencies occur — such as pressure loss, battery fires, and water contamination — triggering an alarm with a 30-to-45-second timer; if time runs out, the mission is immediately terminated. A playthrough can end in three distinct outcomes: mission completed successfully, completed with difficulties, or terminated if oxygen, water, or health reaches zero or radiation reaches one hundred, displaying at the end a logbook with all choices for joint reflection.

The project accurately addresses the challenge of creating a mission trainer for young astronauts by proposing real trade-offs in every decision, integrating with real space weather through queries to the NASA DONKI API, maintaining full data transparency via a space weather dashboard, simulating the real signal delay between Mars and Earth through the Deep Space Network, ensuring high replayability, and providing pedagogical guidelines for teachers. The game's impact encompasses social awareness regarding the urgency of caring for our planet — reinforced by the final message "Teach the children. Shape the future. Save the Earth" —, the stimulation of critical thinking, prioritization, and resource management in education, and bringing children closer to real science and space agency technologies, such as MOXIE, Perseverance, and life support systems.

Regarding the technological resources and tools used in development, TypeScript was the main programming language utilized, while HTML and CSS structured the visuals and screen layouts. The storage of the storyline, choices, translations, and scientific sources was handled in JSON files. The screens and interactivity were built with React, using TanStack Start and Router for navigation, Vite for project execution and bundling, and Tailwind CSS for design and animations. Automated tests for game rules, emergencies, inventory, and languages were executed with Vitest, and code editing was handled in VS Code. Real-world data was obtained through the NASA DONKI API and other sources cited in the credits, while the soundtrack was sourced from Pixabay.com. We also used Artificial Intelligence tools, such as Lovable and Claude, to support technical implementation, assisting in generating and organizing code, building the interface, and creating images and videos. The project requires no special hardware, running smoothly in browsers on computers, tablets, and smartphones.

All decisions regarding the concept, script, in-game choices, aesthetics/design, player experience, objectives, mechanics, and solution validation were led entirely by our team, which also reviewed and adapted all content generated by AI tools to accelerate development without replacing the creative participation of the team members. Throughout the process, we primarily considered the target age group, striving to create an accessible, intuitive, and fun experience for children. We also prioritized the scientific accuracy of the information (based on NASA sources), the balance between difficulty and learning, continuous engagement throughout the entire game, and building an attractive visual interface and compelling narrative.

Using NASA's publicly available scientific resources, our platform allows visitors to explore the Moon, Mars, and deep space, discover historic spacecraft, and learn about their missions, scientific achievements, and challenges.

projectDetails.details:
ETERNOS SPACE: Where Missions End, Discovery Continues

ETERNOS SPACE is an interactive digital space museum developed by Henrique and Guilherme for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026.

Our project was created to address an important educational challenge: how can we preserve the stories of space exploration and make scientific knowledge more accessible, engaging, and meaningful to younger generations?

Space missions may eventually end, but their discoveries, technological achievements, and scientific contributions continue to shape our understanding of the universe.

ETERNOS SPACE transforms this legacy into an immersive educational experience.

Through our platform, visitors can explore missions to the Moon, Mars, and deep space, discover the history of spacecraft, learn about scientific objectives and achievements, and understand the challenges of exploring the universe.

The platform offers interactive timelines, mission profiles, educational content, quizzes, games, and challenges that encourage visitors to actively participate in the learning process.

One of its features is METI, an AI-powered space assistant designed to help users explore astronomy and space science through natural-language conversations.

ETERNOS SPACE also includes a searchable space library, interactive activities, and personalized learning experiences with progress tracking and achievements.

Our goal is to combine reliable space science information with modern digital technology, storytelling, and gamification to inspire curiosity and make space exploration more approachable.

The project draws on NASA's publicly available scientific information and mission resources, connecting educational experiences with the real history of space exploration.

We believe that every spacecraft has a story worth remembering and that the end of a mission should never mean the end of its educational impact.

ETERNOS SPACE is more than a digital museum. It is an invitation to explore, discover, learn, and preserve the extraordinary legacy of humanity's journey beyond Earth.

projectDetails.name: Project The Chess
projectDetails.summary:
Desenvolvemos um Monitor de Saúde de Astronautas: um sistema que acompanha a tripulação durante missões longas, detecta cedo mudanças na saúde de cada pessoa e guia a resposta. Ele abre um caso de acompanhamento e só o encerra quando o problema está resolvido.

O sistema segue um ciclo: medir, detectar, investigar, agir e acompanhar. Sinais vitais, testes de reação, a grade de Amsler (teste de visão), sono, humor e dose de radiação passam por um motor de regras determinístico. Esse motor usa 12 diretivas clínicas, baseadas nos cinco riscos do NASA Human Research Program: radiação, isolamento, distância da Terra, gravidade alterada e ambiente hostil. Cada alerta é classificado como atenção, alerta ou crítico. Um agente de IA roda localmente (Ollama, via MCP) e investiga os casos com 15 ferramentas: cruza sintomas, consulta protocolos e recomenda ações. Ele nunca inventa números nem decide a gravidade. Um painel web mostra a cada astronauta seus indicadores em verde, amarelo ou vermelho e as tarefas do dia, e continua funcionando mesmo sem o agente.

Isso importa porque, a caminho de Marte, o atraso de comunicação impede consultar a equipe médica na Terra em tempo real. A tripulação precisa de autonomia médica confiável, transparente e que funcione offline.
projectDetails.details:
O que ele faz e como funciona

O Monitor de Saúde de Astronautas acompanha a saúde de cada tripulante durante missões de longa duração. Ele detecta alterações cedo e trata cada uma delas como um caso de acompanhamento, do primeiro alerta até a resolução do problema. O sistema funciona em um ciclo contínuo: medir, detectar, investigar, agir, acompanhar e encerrar.

Medir. Os dados vêm de três tipos de fonte: wearables e sensores da nave, simulados (frequência cardíaca, pressão arterial, SpO2, temperatura, dose de radiação, CO2); relatos diários do astronauta (sono, humor, exercício); e autotestes feitos no próprio app. Os autotestes são um teste de tempo de reação, para fadiga cognitiva, e a grade de Amsler, para alterações de visão ligadas à SANS (Síndrome Neuro-Ocular Associada ao Voo Espacial).

Detectar. Um motor de regras determinístico compara cada leitura com o baseline pré-voo do próprio astronauta. Ele faz isso usando 12 diretivas clínicas, baseadas nos cinco riscos do NASA Human Research Program: radiação espacial, isolamento e confinamento, distância da Terra, gravidade alterada e ambientes hostis ou fechados. Cada disparo gera um alerta em um de três níveis: atenção, alerta ou crítico.

Investigar. Alertas de nível alerta ou acima abrem um caso. Um agente de IA local investiga esse caso com 15 ferramentas expostas pelo Model Context Protocol (MCP). Com elas, ele busca telemetria e baselines, consulta a base de conhecimento, cruza sintomas para montar um diagnóstico diferencial, faz perguntas ao astronauta, registra anotações, agenda acompanhamentos, verifica o kit médico e prepara um pacote de relatório autossuficiente para o controle em solo.

Acompanhar e encerrar. O motor reavalia os casos abertos periodicamente. Um caso é encerrado quando os critérios de saída da diretiva são atingidos. Um caso crítico só pode ser encerrado pelo oficial médico da tripulação (CMO) ou pelo médico de voo.

Os astronautas usam um painel web. Nele aparecem seus indicadores em verde, amarelo ou vermelho, as tarefas de saúde do dia, um mapa corporal, gráficos de tendência e os alertas. Também é por ele que registram medições manualmente e fazem os autotestes.

Benefícios

Autonomia médica: a tripulação consegue detectar e conduzir problemas de saúde sem esperar a Terra.

Detecção mais cedo: as leituras são comparadas com o baseline de cada astronauta, e não com uma média populacional. Assim, mudanças pequenas mas relevantes se destacam.

Decisões confiáveis: os níveis de alerta vêm de regras transparentes e auditáveis, escritas em YAML. A IA explica e investiga, mas nunca inventa números nem decide a gravidade.

Cuidado contínuo: toda alteração vira um caso rastreado, com linha do tempo. Nada é detectado e depois esquecido.

Resiliência: o painel continua funcionando offline e sem o agente de IA. Medições manuais ficam salvas no navegador quando o backend está fora do ar.

Impacto pretendido

À medida que as missões saem da ISS rumo à Lua e depois a Marte, o atraso de comunicação passa de cerca de um segundo para muitos minutos. Consultar os médicos de voo em tempo real deixa de ser possível. Nosso projeto explora como uma tripulação pode manter um alto padrão de cuidado por conta própria. A base de conhecimento define como o sistema se adapta a esse atraso: modos assistido, híbrido e autônomo, e pacotes assíncronos e autossuficientes enviados ao solo. A mesma abordagem pode apoiar ambientes remotos e isolados na Terra, como estações na Antártida, submarinos e clínicas em regiões remotas.

Ferramentas, linguagens e software

Linguagens: Python, TypeScript, YAML, JSON e Markdown.

Backend: FastAPI, Uvicorn e SQLite.

Motor de regras: motor determinístico próprio, em Python. Ele lê as diretivas em YAML e valida os dados com JSON Schemas de telemetria, alertas, casos e diretivas.

Agente de IA: LangChain com Ollama, rodando o modelo Qwen 2.5 7B localmente e conectado às ferramentas via MCP (bibliotecas mcp e langchain-mcp-adapters). Rodar localmente reflete o fato de que uma nave não pode depender de conexão com a nuvem.

Frontend: React 19, Vite, Tailwind CSS, Recharts e Framer Motion, com testes em Vitest.

Dados: telemetria simulada de 10 astronautas e 10 cenários (cardíaco, perda óssea, descondicionamento, atrofia muscular, comportamental, térmico, distância, radiação, um cenário original e um controle saudável). Um script de replay transmite um cenário "ao vivo" para ver um caso abrir e escalar.

Hardware: nenhum dedicado. Tudo roda em um notebook comum, com os sensores simulados.

O que torna o projeto criativo

Regras decidem, IA investiga: separamos a detecção determinística do raciocínio da IA. Assim, o sistema ganha a flexibilidade de um modelo de linguagem sem deixá-lo tomar decisões críticas de segurança.

Base de conhecimento como fonte única: um mesmo conjunto de arquivos (diretivas, documentação dos riscos, índice de sintomas, protocolos e o prompt do agente) alimenta tanto o motor de regras quanto o agente de IA, sem duplicação.

Operação consciente do atraso: o painel considera o ambiente da missão (ISS, Lua ou trânsito para Marte) e o atraso de comunicação de cada um.

Autotestes no app: testes simples, como o de tempo de reação e a grade de Amsler, transformam o astronauta em um sensor ativo para problemas que os wearables não captam.

Gamificação cooperativa: pontos de experiência, sequências de dias, medalhas e metas da tripulação incentivam medições diárias consistentes. Os pontos são sempre somados para a tripulação e, de propósito, não existe ranking entre astronautas.

Fatores que a equipe considerou

Segurança e responsabilidade: a IA não pode disparar nem descartar alertas, casos críticos exigem aval humano, e a cadeia de escalonamento segue protocolos definidos.

Atraso de comunicação e operação offline: IA local, painel que funciona offline e relatórios autossuficientes para o solo.

Privacidade: diretivas de saúde comportamental são marcadas como restritas. Dados psicológicos vão só para o médico de voo ou o psicólogo, e o agente nunca rotula diagnósticos psiquiátricos.

Usabilidade sob estresse: código de cores tipo semáforo, explicações em linguagem simples e rotinas diárias curtas.

Base científica: as diretivas seguem o modelo de riscos do Human Research Program da NASA e suas evidências.

Limitações assumidas: é um protótipo educacional, não um dispositivo médico. Os dados são simulados, e os limiares são valores de referência apenas para o protótipo.

projectDetails.name: Orbit Sentinel - Protecting Human Life Beyond Earth
projectDetails.summary:
What happens when an astronaut faces a health emergency millions of kilometers from Earth, where even a message to mission control can take 20 minutes to arrive?

Orbit Sentinel was created to help bridge that critical gap.

Orbit Sentinel is a wearable-oriented astronaut health-monitoring platform designed to transform complex health and environmental information into actionable insights, empowering crews to monitor their well-being and make informed decisions during deep-space missions.

Addressing NASA's five major human spaceflight hazards, our system brings together radiation exposure, mental health, sleep quality, cardiovascular indicators, physical conditioning, gravity adaptation, spacecraft environmental conditions, health guides, and communication delays in one intuitive interface.

Our proposed architecture incorporates NASA's RadLab scientific datasets to support radiation monitoring, while interactive dashboards, symptom reporting, preventive recommendations, and protective guidance demonstrate how astronauts could recognize potential risks and respond more independently.

Our innovation is not another health dashboard. It is a step toward an integrated, autonomous health-support ecosystem for human space exploration.

From the Moon to Mars and beyond, Orbit Sentinel envisions a future where distance from Earth does not mean distance from essential health information.

Orbit Sentinel - Protecting the explorers. Empowering the future.
projectDetails.details:
1) Introduction

Protecting the explorers. Empowering the future.

Space exploration is not only about how far humanity can go, but how well we can protect those who take us there. As astronauts venture into deep space, they face challenges that extend far beyond Earth: radiation exposure, altered gravity, physical deterioration, sleep disruption, and psychological stress. With limited access to immediate medical support, monitoring their own health becomes essential. Orbit Sentinel is an astronaut health monitoring platform designed to bring these critical indicators together in one intelligent interface. By tracking vital signs, radiation exposure, sleep, mental well-being, and physical performance, while connecting gravitational conditions to the body's adaptation, it helps astronauts understand their health, recognize potential risks, and make informed decisions throughout their missions.

Because the future of space exploration depends not only on reaching new worlds, but on keeping humanity healthy enough to explore them.

2) Radiation

Space radiation is one of the most significant health challenges in human space exploration, particularly during long-duration missions to the Moon and Mars. Orbit Sentinel doesn't just monitor radiation. It helps astronauts understand exposure, respond to alerts, and follow protective procedures, even when Earth is far away. Is designed to transform scientific radiation measurements into actionable health-monitoring information, combining NASA radiation datasets, automated data processing, exposure visualization, and mission-specific safety guidance.

2.1. Integration with NASA Radiation Data - Real Scientific Measurements

Orbit Sentinel's proposed radiation monitoring architecture integrates with NASA's Radiation Laboratory (RadLab) API, part of NASA's Open Science Data Repository ecosystem. This integration enables the application to retrieve historical radiation measurements collected by scientific instruments aboard spacecraft, including the International Space Station (ISS). Using NASA's documented API, the system can query radiation data according to spacecraft, instrument, measurement type, and observation period.

2.2 Example NASA API endpoint:

https://visualization.osdr.nasa.gov/radlab/api/?spacecraft=ISS&instrument=DosTel&timestamp%3E=2022-04-01T23%3A00&timestamp%3C2022-04-02T01%3A05&dose_equivalent_rate&format=json

This request is designed to retrieve dose-equivalent-rate measurements from the DosTel instrument for a specified historical period. By incorporating NASA's scientific datasets, Orbit Sentinel aims to demonstrate how actual space radiation observations can support astronaut health-monitoring applications, reducing dependence on exclusively simulated measurements.

2.3 Radiation Data Processing - Backend Architecture

Orbit Sentinel uses a proposed backend architecture to process, standardize, and organize radiation measurements. The backend acts as an intermediary between external scientific data sources and the astronaut-facing monitoring interface. Its processing workflow consists of five stages:

  1. Data Acquisition: Retrieve radiation measurements from NASA RadLab or other compatible sources.
  2. Data Validation: Verify measurement availability, timestamps, units, instrument identification, and data integrity.
  3. Unit Standardization: Convert compatible radiation measurements into standardized units for consistent presentation.
  4. Exposure Monitoring: Organize measurements into historical time series and calculate exposure trends.
  5. API Distribution: Deliver structured JSON responses to the Orbit Sentinel dashboard.

This modular architecture is intended to support additional radiation monitoring instruments in the future, including compatible personal dosimeters and spacecraft radiation sensors, subject to their communication protocols and data-access permissions.

2.4 Radiation Calculations - Transforming Scientific Data into Structured JSON

One of Orbit Sentinel's key technical capabilities is its proposed radiation data-processing pipeline. NASA RadLab can provide dose-equivalent-rate measurements expressed in microsieverts per hour (µSv/h). When this measurement is available, the Laravel backend converts it into millisieverts per hour (mSv/h) using the following equation: Dose Rate (mSv/h) = Dose Rate (µSv/h) / 1,000

For example, a hypothetical measurement of 14 µSv/h produces: 14 / 1,000 = 0.014 mSv/h

This standardized measurement can then be displayed in the astronaut's radiation monitoring dashboard. For time-series measurements, accumulated dose can be estimated by integrating the dose-equivalent rate over time: Accumulated Dose (mSv) ≈ Σ [Dose Rate (mSv/h) × Time Interval (hours)]

This calculation requires valid measurement intervals and consistent dosimetric quantities. It does not automatically represent an astronaut's total mission exposure unless the relevant personal exposure history is available. After processing, the backend is designed to expose a standardized REST endpoint:

GET /api/radiation/latest

Example JSON response: {  "source": "nasa_radlab",  "spacecraft": "ISS",  "instrument": DosTel",  "measurement": { "quantity": "dose_equivalent_rate", "value": 0.014, "unit": "mSv/h"  },  "mission_dose_mSv": null,  "status": "not_evaluated",  "sensor_status": "unknown",  "alert": null,  "data_mode": "historical",  "is_simulated": false}

This JSON illustrates the proposed data transformation using a hypothetical measurement, not a verified API response.

The structured response allows the frontend to consume radiation information independently of the original scientific data format. It also distinguishes historical measurements from simulated data and avoids assigning safety classifications when validated mission-specific thresholds are unavailable.

2.5 Radiation Monitoring and Astronaut Decision Support

Orbit Sentinel is designed to go beyond radiation data visualization by connecting exposure measurements with astronaut health-monitoring workflows. Its radiation monitoring interface is structured around four complementary capabilities:

2.6 Continuous Exposure Visualization

Display the latest available radiation measurements, historical trends, and accumulated exposure when sufficient data exists.

2.7 Radiation Alerts

Evaluate incoming measurements against configurable, mission-approved exposure criteria and identify potentially abnormal changes. In the demonstration environment, simulated radiation events can trigger illustrative alerts without representing operational NASA safety thresholds.

2.8 Health Symptom Reporting

Connect radiation monitoring with the Orbit Sentinel Report Symptoms module, enabling astronauts to document symptoms, record their onset and severity, and associate reports with available exposure measurements for subsequent medical review.

The application does not assume that symptoms are caused by radiation exposure and does not replace medical diagnosis or mission medical protocols.

2.9 Protective Action Guidance

Provide astronauts with offline-accessible guidance based on mission-approved radiation protection procedures, including shelter instructions and communication protocols during potential radiation events.

2.10 Technical Innovation and Mission Impact

The central innovation of Orbit Sentinel is not the radiation sensor itself, but the software architecture that transforms complex scientific measurements into accessible information for astronaut health monitoring. Orbit Sentinel's vision is to turn space radiation data into meaningful, timely, and actionable information, helping astronauts monitor their exposure, recognize potential hazards, and follow appropriate protective procedures during missions beyond Earth.

3) Isolation and Confinement

During long-duration space missions, astronauts face significant behavioral and psychological challenges caused by prolonged isolation, confinement in limited spaces, and separation from Earth. To address these challenges, Orbit Sentinel integrates digital tools designed to monitor mental well-being, sleep patterns, emotional states, and fatigue. Through daily check-ins, visual health indicators, and personalized recommendations, the platform helps astronauts recognize behavioral changes, maintain healthy routines, and take preventive action. Our goal is to transform health monitoring into proactive support, strengthening astronaut resilience, well-being, and autonomy throughout deep-space missions.

3.1 Sleep Monitoring - Last Night

Orbit Sentinel provides a detailed overview of the astronaut's latest sleep cycle, including total sleep duration, sleep quality, and estimated sleep stages (Deep, Light, REM, and Awake). The system highlights irregular sleep routines and offers practical recommendations to encourage consistent rest patterns, helping astronauts recognize potential sleep-related risks during prolonged missions.

3.2 Sleep Trends - 7-Day Analysis

The seven-day dashboard tracks sleep duration over time, displaying average sleep hours, daily variations, and progress toward rest goals. Visual trends help astronauts identify changes in their sleeping habits, while contextual recommendations encourage healthier routines and greater awareness of potential fatigue.

3.3 Daily Check-in - Emotional Self-Assessment

A simple, intuitive interface allows astronauts to record how they feel through five emotional states: Great, Good, Normal, Tired, and Bad. Additional fields capture energy levels and physical symptoms, creating a daily record of self-reported health that can help astronauts recognize changes in their emotional and physical condition.

3.4 Mental Health - Psychological Well-being

Orbit Sentinel brings together four essential psychological indicators: Mood, Stress, Fatigue, and Focus, presented through an intuitive well-being dashboard. A visual well-being score provides a quick overview of the astronaut's reported mental state, supporting self-awareness and encouraging regular emotional check-ins. By tracking these indicators over time, the system aims to help astronauts recognize early signs of psychological strain associated with isolation and confinement.

Our Goal: Transform daily health observations into meaningful insights, helping astronauts maintain emotional resilience, healthy sleep routines, and psychological well-being throughout long-duration space missions.

4) Distance from Earth

As astronauts travel farther from Earth, communication delays increase, reducing the ability of mission control teams to provide immediate assistance during medical emergencies. This challenge becomes particularly significant during long-duration missions to Mars, where one-way communication delays can reach approximately 20 minutes. Orbit Sentinel addresses this NASA Human Research Program hazard by providing a simulated Distance from Earth monitoring module that demonstrates how increasing distance affects communication availability and astronaut autonomy.

The goal is to transform mission-distance scenarios into meaningful operational information, helping astronauts understand communication limitations and the importance of autonomous decision-making during deep-space missions.

4.1 NASA Hazard Alignment - Distance from Earth

According to NASA's Human Research Program, distance from Earth introduces significant challenges to human space exploration, including delayed communication, limited access to immediate medical support, equipment failures, and the need for greater crew self-sufficiency.

The module focuses on two primary indicators:

a) Earth Distance: Represents the simulated distance between the spacecraft and Earth, displayed in miles.

b) One-Way Signal Delay: Represents the estimated time required for a radio signal to travel from the spacecraft to Earth, based on the simulated distance and the speed of light.

Orbit Sentinel uses this hazard as the foundation for its Distance from Earth module.

Orbit Sentinel provides an interactive mission dashboard that visualizes the spacecraft's journey between Earth and Mars, displaying distance traveled, remaining distance, estimated arrival time, and one-way communication delay.

5) Gravity Fields

During space missions, astronauts must adapt to different gravitational environments, from microgravity during spaceflight to the partial gravity of Mars. These changes can affect muscle strength, bone density, balance, coordination, and cardiovascular function. To address these challenges, Orbit Sentinel provides integrated tools designed to monitor physical condition, track exercise routines, and support adaptation to changing gravity. Through visual health indicators, activity tracking, and preventive recommendations, the platform helps astronauts maintain physical readiness and recognize potential changes in their condition.

Our goal is to support physical resilience, reduce the risks associated with altered gravity, and help astronauts remain healthy and mission-ready throughout their journey.

5.1 Physical Condition - Health and Performance Monitoring

Orbit Sentinel provides a unified overview of the astronaut's physical condition, including exercise load, muscle and bone status, balance, and cardiovascular capacity. A seven-day activity chart helps visualize physical performance trends, while clear status indicators allow astronauts to quickly assess their condition and maintain awareness of their physical readiness.

5.2 Bone & Balance - Musculoskeletal Health

In reduced gravity, maintaining muscle strength and bone health becomes essential. Orbit Sentinel tracks resistance exercise sessions, displays completed and planned activities, and provides indicators for bone loading and muscle condition. By organizing exercise routines and monitoring activity consistency, the platform supports astronauts in maintaining musculoskeletal health and following their physical conditioning plans.

5.3 Gravity Fields - Adaptation to Martian Gravity

Transitioning between gravitational environments presents unique challenges for astronaut health and mobility. Orbit Sentinel includes a dedicated gravity adaptation dashboard that displays the current mission environment, including Mars' gravitational acceleration of approximately 0.38 g.bThe interface highlights four key adaptation areas: Balance, Coordination, Muscle Strength, and Bone Health, providing a consolidated overview of physical readiness.

Preventive recommendations encourage regular exercise and awareness of symptoms such as dizziness or balance difficulties, supporting safer adaptation to partial-gravity environments.

6) Hostile/Closed Environments

During long-duration space missions, maintaining a safe and healthy environment inside a spacecraft is essential. Astronauts face challenges related to air quality, atmospheric pressure, temperature, microbial contamination, lighting, and noise, all of which can affect their health and performance. To address these challenges, Orbit Sentinel introduces a dedicated habitat monitoring dashboard designed to provide astronauts with a clear overview of their living environment.

6.1 Habitat Environment - Environmental Health Monitoring

Orbit Sentinel brings together essential environmental indicators in a single, intuitive interface:

  • Air Quality: Displays oxygen (O₂) and carbon dioxide (CO₂) levels to support awareness of atmospheric conditions.
  • Cabin Conditions: Presents temperature and atmospheric pressure readings to help astronauts assess their living environment.
  • Microbial Monitoring: Provides visibility into the monitoring status of microbial conditions in cabin air and surfaces.
  • Lighting & Noise: Displays environmental status indicators related to crew comfort and well-being.

Through clear visual indicators and environmental status summaries, the platform helps astronauts quickly recognize potential changes in habitat conditions.

Our goal is to transform complex environmental information into accessible insights, supporting astronaut safety, environmental awareness, and informed decision-making during deep-space missions.

projectDetails.name: RasterRoot – Intelligent Crop Rotation System
projectDetails.summary:
RasterRoot is a mobile, user-friendly and easy to use decision-support application designed to help farmers plan the crop rotation strategies. 
By integrating NASA Earth observation data, local farm information, and agronomic criteria, the platform uses a multi-criteria analysis model to recommend sustainable and productive cropping systems. 
Farmers can map fields, and with the app evaluation of the climate and water conditions, compare different rotation scenarios based on factors such as water availability, soil health, erosion risk, crop diversification, vegetation cover, operational feasibility, and economic potential. 
Initially focused on Uberlândia and the Triângulo Mineiro region in Brazil, RasterRoot aims to transform complex scientific data into accessible insights that support better agricultural decisions. 
The project promotes sustainable land management, increases resilience to climate change, and helps producers balance productivity with environmental conservation, contributing to a smarter and more climate-adaptive future for agriculture.
projectDetails.details:
Problem

Climate change is making agricultural decision-making increasingly complex. Rising temperatures, irregular rainfall patterns, prolonged droughts, and soil degradation directly affect crop productivity, water availability, and long-term farm sustainability. Choosing unsuitable crops or crop sequences can accelerate nutrient depletion, increase erosion risks, and reduce resilience to environmental challenges. Small and medium-sized farmers often face additional barriers, including limited access to environmental data, technical assistance, and planning tools. Although scientific information and Earth observation data exist, they are not always accessible or easy to interpret for practical farm management. There is a growing need for a solution that integrates climate, environmental, and agronomic information into a user-friendly platform capable of evaluating crop rotation alternatives based on local conditions.

Proposed Solution

RasterRoot is a mobile decision-support platform that transforms NASA environmental data, local farm information, and agronomic knowledge into actionable agricultural insights. Using a multi-criteria scoring system, the application compares current crop rotation practices with alternative strategies, highlighting potential benefits, risks, and operational constraints for each option.

The platform helps farmers identify opportunities for diversification, water conservation, soil protection, vegetation cover improvement, and sustainable land management while respecting their operational priorities and production goals. Recommendations are presented in a clear and accessible format and are intended to support, rather than replace, farmers' expertise and professional agronomic assessments.

How It Works

Farmers begin by registering key property information, including location, field size, main crops, current rotation practices, irrigation methods, and agricultural priorities. Using GPS or manual map drawing tools, users define the field boundaries to be analyzed. The application calculates the area, processes geographic coordinates, and evaluates environmental indicators. Results are displayed through an intuitive interface featuring rankings, scores, environmental metrics, visual charts, risk alerts, and confidence indicators. Users can also generate and share technical reports.

Key Features

  • Farm registration and management.
  • Field mapping and boundary delineation.
  • Automatic area calculation and geospatial analysis.
  • Comparison of crop rotation scenarios through multi-criteria evaluation.
  • Environmental indicators related to water availability, soil health, erosion risk, and vegetation cover.
  • Interactive charts, rankings, strengths, and warning alerts.
  • Satellite map visualization and environmental layers.
  • Technical report generation and sharing.
  • Portuguese and English language support.
  • Offline storage of up to 20 analyzed fields for later consultation.

By making scientific and Earth observation data accessible to farmers, RasterRoot aims to promote sustainable agriculture, improve climate resilience, and support smarter land-use decisions, initially focusing on Uberlândia and the Triângulo Mineiro region of Brazil.

projectDetails.name: Mission Mars Game
projectDetails.summary: Mission Mars is a browser-based mission trainer that lets a child run a Mars colony for eleven sols. Five resources — water, oxygen, energy, food and materials — rise and fall in real time while the colony moves through 90-second days and nights. Twenty-five events, from dust storms and marsquakes to crew conflicts, appear in a Mission Log with four trade-off choices each, and ignoring one has its own consequence. Buildings have levels and build timers, research takes time, robots explore the surface and can break down, and a radio link to Houston answers 15 to 20 seconds late, the way real deep-space communication does. Every event, site and term is tagged with the open NASA source behind it: DONKI space weather, OSDR life sciences, Perseverance, Curiosity, InSight and SCaN. Losing opens a science debriefing instead of a "game over", so failure becomes a lesson. Three difficulty modes let younger and older players train at their own pace. Mars is the hook; systems thinking is the lesson.
projectDetails.details:
What it does and how it works. Mission Mars is a browser-based mission trainer where a child commands a Mars colony for eleven sols. The screen is a mission control center: a header with the mission clock and a day/night indicator, a COLONY RESOURCES panel with five live bars — water, oxygen, energy, food and materials — and a Mission Log that is the heart of the game. Every event appears there as a large Mars image, a timestamp, a short narrative and four big decision buttons. Time runs on a fixed cycle: 90 seconds of daylight and 90 seconds of night, three minutes per sol. Solar panels produce energy only in daylight, batteries carry the base through the night, and the crew keeps consuming water, oxygen and food the whole time. Twenty-five events are drawn at random and weighted toward pressure — 20% opportunities, 40% dilemmas, 40% crises — and every one of them has four choices with real trade-offs, hidden risks and a consequence if the player ignores the event for 60 seconds. Buildings have five levels and take time to build or upgrade. Ten research technologies reach three levels each and cost 30, 60 or 90 seconds per level. Robots with 100 hit points are built, sent to twenty real Martian sites such as Jezero Crater, Gale Crater, Utopia Planitia and Olympus Mons, and can break down and be repaired or lost. A radio link to Houston costs energy and answers 15 to 20 seconds late, the way deep-space communication really works. Winning means surviving to sol 11 and returning to Earth; losing opens a science debriefing that explains the cause, what was learned and one tip for the next flight.

Benefits and intended impact. The game teaches systems thinking: saving energy can starve oxygen, a fast trip can cost a robot, and a party raises morale but eats the food stores. Children practice reading trends, comparing costs and asking for help before an emergency grows — with no penalty for failing, because every loss is explained. It also makes open NASA data a story kids can touch, and it runs in any browser on a school computer or tablet with nothing to install.

Tools and languages. React 19 with TypeScript and TanStack Start, styled with Tailwind CSS v4. The whole simulation is one pure reducer in a single engine file, so every tab reads the same state and every rule can be unit-tested; 106 automated tests cover resource flow, death rules, research, robots, exploration, radio support and difficulty. Event art is generated imagery, and the project was built and iterated with Lovable.

What makes it creative. Instead of a quiz or a score, failure is rewritten as a debriefing; instead of instant answers, the radio reproduces real signal latency; instead of a "correct" option, each choice is only better or worse for the colony you actually have.

Factors considered. Difficulty for ages 7–12 without unfair punishment, honest sourcing of NASA data, screen simplicity and large touch targets, three difficulty modes, and no names, faces or voices of anyone under 18 anywhere in the project.

The file also has a ≈250-word version, the NASA data links for those fields, and a pre-paste checklist. I ran the tests to confirm the numbers quoted: 106 passing, 25 events, 20 sites, 10 researches, 8 buildings, 15–20 s radio delay.
