projectDetails.name: Atlas | Stars & Beyond: preventing fire in microgravity environments
projectDetails.summary:
We are Team Stars & Beyond, driven by the mission to make space exploration safer and democratize access to scientific knowledge about how fire behaves beyond Earth.
To achieve this, we developed Atlas Stars & Beyond (Extinction Atlas), an interactive scientific intelligence platform that consolidates decades of microgravity combustion research from NASA's Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) repository. Atlas maps documented experiments across oxygen concentrations, atmospheric pressures, and gravity regimes, connecting researchers, students, and engineers to critical experimental evidence with full file- and row-level traceability.
By making existing evidence accessible while explicitly revealing where experimental data is missing, Atlas accelerates the investigation of fire prevention and suppression strategies for future space missions.
projectDetails.details:
Atlas Stars & Beyond is a scientific intelligence and visualization platform developed for the NASA Space Apps Challenge (Flame in Freefall). Its purpose is to transform decades of microgravity combustion research into accessible, interactive, and actionable engineering knowledge.

The platform addresses the challenge of fragmented aerospace fire safety data by bringing together experimental records, deterministic physical calculations, multidimensional data visualization, and a real-time WebGL2 3D combustion solver within a unified analytical environment.

By combining Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), deterministic evidence rules implemented in Go, interactive dataset exploration, and real-time 3D visualization, Atlas enables researchers and engineers to investigate hypotheses across different spacecraft habitats and materials. Users can adjust environmental parameters—including gravity regimes, atmospheric pressure, and oxygen concentration—to assess experimental coverage, compare fire suppression strategies (such as CO₂ and helium), and examine scientific evidence with full source traceability down to the original file and row.

Beyond retrieving existing literature, Atlas functions as a discovery engine for space fire safety. Through interactive 3D test maps, evidence knowledge graphs, flammability limit visualizations, and the Next Fire gap-analysis queue, the platform reveals underexplored physical conditions—such as partial gravity on the Moon and Mars—and identifies promising directions for future experiments.

By bridging historical NASA datasets with interactive simulation and evidence-grounded AI synthesis, Atlas accelerates scientific investigation and supports the development of safer fire prevention and suppression protocols for future long-duration space missions.


Repository Access – GitHub

Organization: https://github.com/stars-beyond

Backend & Data Pipelines: https://github.com/stars-beyond/atlas-fire-extintion-backend

Frontend & 3D Lab: https://github.com/stars-beyond/atlas-fire-extintion-front


The Problem

Over several decades, NASA has conducted thousands of experiments and published extensive research on fire behavior in microgravity environments, including 24 combustion investigations available through the NASA Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) system.

Despite the critical importance of this knowledge for crewed mission safety, the sheer volume of research—and its distribution across heterogeneous tables, PDFs, and technical reports—makes it difficult to retrieve, interpret, and compare experimental findings.

Researchers and engineers must spend considerable time searching and cross-referencing studies to understand how different materials, atmospheric compositions, and ventilation conditions influence combustion. This fragmentation also makes it harder to identify patterns, compare experimental outcomes, and recognize scientific gaps, limiting the ability of existing research to guide future investigations.


The Gap

Advances in artificial intelligence, data engineering, and real-time browser-based simulation create new opportunities to explore large scientific archives. However, a generic chatbot built on top of PDFs is not sufficient for aerospace fire safety: it cannot reliably guarantee source traceability, distinguish measured outcomes from extrapolations, or reveal where experimental evidence is simply unavailable.

For example, future lunar habitats are expected to operate at oxygen concentrations of 30% or higher and atmospheric pressures of 10.2 psi or lower. However, solid-material combustion tests in the NASA PSI archive were conducted at oxygen concentrations ranging from 13.6% to 22.2%, near 1 atm. Furthermore, PSI contains no combustion tests conducted under partial-gravity conditions representative of the Moon or Mars.

This reveals a critical gap between the availability of historical experimental data and the ability to analyze it systematically—making both existing evidence and missing experimental conditions immediately visible.


Our Solution

Atlas is an integrated platform that enables users to investigate, analyze, compare, and explore fire behavior across diverse space environments.

Its backend consolidates 24 NASA PSI combustion investigations, comprising 1,972 tabulated tests (1,153 of which include oxygen and pressure metadata), a hybrid PostgreSQL + pgvector search index, a deterministic evidence engine implemented in Go, and a RAG pipeline containing 18,436 indexed document chunks from NASA PSI and NTRS.

Rather than generating unsupported risk scores, Atlas computes a transparent, four-level Evidence Verdict for each scenario:

Measured: Experimental tests are available under the target atmospheric conditions (±2% O₂ and ±20% pressure) and gravity regime.

Bounded: No tests exist at the exact gravity level, but experimental data is available at both 0 g and 1 g under comparable atmospheric conditions, providing bounds for analysis.

One-sided: Experimental tests are available at only one of the two reference gravity levels (0 g or 1 g).

Terra Incognita: No NASA PSI experimental tests are available under the target atmospheric conditions.

When experimental evidence exists (Measured), Atlas reports empirical outcomes directly, such as the number of samples that burned completely, self-extinguished, or failed to ignite.

When experimental evidence is unavailable, the platform does not fabricate probabilities or unsupported conclusions. Instead, it clearly communicates the limits of existing knowledge: AI generates the explanation, while the underlying data determines the verdict.


How It Works

When users access Atlas, they can explore the platform through a guided configurator (Test Drive) or navigate directly to its analytical modules.

1. Habitat & Free-Text Inference

Users can select from six preset environments: Space Station, Lunar Base, Rover, Mars Habitat, Spacesuit, or Earth Room. Alternatively, they can manually adjust oxygen concentration, atmospheric pressure, and gravity.

A natural-language input—for example, "lunar rover with 34% oxygen and Nomex seats"—automatically extracts the relevant parameters and configures the Test Drive.

2. Material Selection

Users select a fuel family and material, including cotton fabric, acrylic/PMMA, Nomex, silicone, liquid fuels, or gases. For each selection, Atlas displays the exact number of NASA experiments available.

3. Test Drive & Interactive 3D Stage

Clicking Light activates the flame in the 3D environment and reveals the four-level Evidence Verdict.

Three tabs guide the investigation:

Evidence: Displays the verdict, empirical rates, and the closest matching NASA experiments. Selecting a test opens its exact source file, row, and original experimental record.

Extinguish: Allows users to release CO₂ or helium, reduce cabin ventilation, and examine FLEX droplet burn-rate regressions and extinction behavior.

Ask: Provides a natural-language scientific Q&A interface powered by RAG, featuring Server-Sent Events (SSE) streaming, clickable numbered citations, rendered LaTeX equations, and source page references.

4. Multi-View Stage

The main visualization area seamlessly switches between multiple analytical environments:

3D Combustion Lab (lab3d): A real-time WebGL2 3D combustion visualization.

3D Test Map: Maps experimental coverage across gravity regimes, with each floor representing a different gravity condition and visibly exposing empty Moon and Mars floors.

Knowledge Graph: Connects the selected scenario to related experiments, revealing relationships between experimental conditions and available evidence.

Flammability Limits: Provides an interactive view of flammability boundaries.

Thermal Camera: An ONNX-powered prediction tool for PMMA film flame spread.

5. Technical Dossier, Dashboard & Mission Story

Atlas also provides tools for deeper scientific investigation and reporting:

Technical Dossier: Generates downloadable Markdown or printable reports containing relevant technical findings.

Scientific Intelligence Dashboard: Allows users to build custom scatter plots, bar charts, and histograms using 15 API datasets, with CSV/PNG export and row-level drill-down.

Investigation Comparison: Enables side-by-side analysis of different experimental investigations.

Next Fire: Presents a gap-analysis queue highlighting opportunities for future experiments.

Mission Story: Offers interactive 3D mission scenarios powered by precomputed trajectories from mission-fire-engine.

Implementation Details

DATA PIPELINES

Data ingestion and preparation are handled by modular Python pipelines (brain/atlas/ and ml/):

Sources (psi.py): Retrieves combustion investigations, catalogs, and experimental tables from NASA PSI, with local caching and an offline seed fallback (data/seed/).

Adapters (adapters.py): Uses table-specific normalization adapters to map heterogeneous experimental records into a unified schema while preserving original file names, line numbers, raw records, and explicit flags for inferred fields (such as assuming a cabin pressure of 1 atm for solid-material tests when the original value is not specified).

Documents & Embeddings (docs.py, rag-index): Extracts text from NASA PSI PDFs and challenge resources using PyMuPDF and pypdf. Atlas documents are embedded locally using fastembed, while the RAG collection (flame_freefall_2026_v6) indexes 18,436 chunks from NASA PSI and NTRS in PostgreSQL + pgvector using OpenAI's text-embedding-3-large.

ML & Thermal Models (ml/): Includes cross-validated linear regression for FLEX droplet burn rates, as well as scripts (spread_table.py, export_thermal.py) that export Atlas-MachineL neural models into lookup grids and ONNX networks for predicting PMMA film spread speed and surface temperature under 0 g conditions.

BACKEND

API (api/, Go 1.25): A domain-driven Go service covering evidence, catalog, flammability, prediction, Q&A, search, datasets, and simulation modules. Connected to PostgreSQL via pgx/v5, it computes all deterministic verdicts, investigation rankings, empirical burn rates, flammability assessments, knowledge graph topologies, dataset charts, and hybrid RRF search. It also proxies SSE-based Q&A streaming (/api/ask/stream) to the RAG service, with graceful fallback to Anthropic Claude, OpenAI-compatible endpoints, or extractive mode when API keys are unavailable.

RAG Service (rag/, Python + FastAPI): Runs the team's rag-Carlin pipeline, adapted to PostgreSQL + pgvector (atlas_pg/), delivering evidence-grounded answers with numbered citations, reviewed equations, and conversation history.

Embedder Service (brain/, Python + FastAPI): Generates query embeddings through fastembed and executes ONNX-based thermal camera inference using onnxruntime.

FRONTEND

Stack: Built with React 18, TypeScript, Vite, Three.js, Recharts, react-markdown, remark-math, and rehype-katex. The architecture is organized by feature (configurator, stage, ask, findings, investigations, next-fire, dashboard, and story), with no scientific computations performed on the client side. Every verdict, ranking, and chart calculation is handled by the Go API.

3D Combustion Lab (public/lab3d/): A real-time WebGL2 GPU combustion solver embedded through an iframe bridge (bridge.js) that receives physical constants and scenario parameters from /api/sim/config. The model is an uncalibrated study visualization, clearly labeled as such in the interface and kept strictly independent of the Evidence Verdict.

Deployment: Published as static assets on Cloudflare Workers & Pages (wrangler.jsonc), communicating with the Go API over HTTPS/CORS.

INFRASTRUCTURE

Containerization: Orchestrated through Docker and Docker Compose (docker-compose.yml), running the database (pgvector/pgvector:pg16), embedder, ingestion pipeline (with fingerprint-based atomic schema swapping from atlas_build to atlas), RAG indexing, RAG service, and API.

Production: Deployed behind Nginx and Cloudflare, with automated daily NASA PSI data refreshes through deploy/refresh.sh.

Impact

Atlas transforms complex, fragmented aerospace combustion research into accessible, traceable, and actionable engineering intelligence. By enabling researchers and engineers to compare experiments, visualize evidence coverage, identify knowledge gaps, and inspect original experimental records, the platform makes decades of NASA microgravity research more accessible and useful for future investigations.

Its scientific contribution goes beyond organizing existing data. Atlas helps reveal what current experiments can—and cannot—support, highlights underexplored conditions such as partial gravity and elevated-oxygen exploration atmospheres, and helps prioritize future experiments that could address the most significant knowledge gaps.

In practical terms, this means researchers can investigate scenarios more efficiently, identify where additional testing is needed, and make better-informed decisions when designing future experiments and fire suppression strategies.

The platform also has potential applications beyond aerospace research, including terrestrial environments such as enclosed battery rooms under 1 g conditions. By maintaining a clear distinction between experimental evidence, deterministic analysis, and exploratory simulation, Atlas supports evidence-based technical investigation without presenting itself as a flight-safety certification system.

Ultimately, Atlas helps turn fragmented scientific archives into a practical foundation for identifying risks, directing research efforts, and advancing fire safety in environments where reliable experimental knowledge is essential.

Atlas Stars & Beyond brings together deterministic engineering logic, multidimensional data visualization, real-time 3D simulation, and evidence-grounded AI to bridge the gap between historical microgravity combustion research and the challenges of future space exploration.

By making both experimental findings and their limitations visible, Atlas transforms how researchers access, interpret, and investigate scientific evidence. Its approach empowers a new generation of researchers and engineers to identify knowledge gaps, guide future experiments, and contribute to the development of safer habitats beyond Earth.

projectDetails.name: Apogeu
projectDetails.summary: We developed a free, browser-based 2D strategy game set in the Cold War space race (1955–1969). Each player runs a space agency (USA or USSR side) racing to complete a ladder of historical missions. A dice-driven circular board provides resources, buildings, shops, espionage and chance events — but the heart of the game is the engineering workshop: players design their spacecraft by choosing a launch vehicle, orbit, instruments and parts, each with explicit trade-offs in cost, mass, power, data and risk, then decide the central dilemma — launch now, cheap and risky, or wait and let rivals pull ahead. Launches are simulated stage by stage, and every failure comes with a clear explanation of why it happened, plus a "In real history" card connecting it to actual events. This addresses the challenge directly: players define mission goals, design under constraints, simulate, and learn from feedback. It matters because it makes real mission-design reasoning — budgets, trade-offs, risk — accessible and fun for beginners and youth, solo or with up to four players, with no installation required.
projectDetails.details:
What it does / how it works: A browser-based 2D board game where 1–4 players each run a space agency (US/USSR) during the 1955–1969 space race. Gameplay alternates between a shared circular board (dice movement, buildings, shops, espionage, chance events, rival bots) and an engineering workshop where players design spacecraft — picking launch vehicles, orbits, instruments, and parts, each with explicit cost/mass/power/data/risk trade-offs. Each turn, players choose to research, build, upgrade, or attempt launch. Launches run through a staged simulation (src/sim/simulate.js, flight.js) that computes success/failure with transparent causes, tied to a historical "In real history" card. Years advance in 3-round cycles (1955→1969), building a ladder of missions players race to complete first.

Benefits: No installs, no cost, runs entirely in-browser; supports solo (sandbox) or hot-seat/networked multiplayer up to 4; teaches real mission-design reasoning (budget, mass, power, data, risk) through consequence rather than lecture; failure is explained, not just penalized, turning mistakes into learning moments.

Intended impact: Make space mission engineering trade-offs approachable and engaging for beginners/youth, per the challenge's goal of broadening access to mission design concepts, while also teaching real space race history.

Tools/languages: Plain JavaScript (ES modules), no build step/framework, node --test for testing; custom peer-to-peer networking (src/net/peer.js, lobby.js, sync.js, roomCode.js) for multiplayer; HTML/CSS for UI/rendering (src/ui/*, src/board/board.js).

Creativity: Combines a Monopoly-style board (resource/social layer) with a serious engineering/simulation layer underneath; frames the core tension as "launch now (cheap, risky) vs. wait (safer, rivals advance)"; adds narrative texture via espionage, rumors, dilemma cards, and historical callouts tying game outcomes to real Cold War space history.

Factors considered: Every mechanic was checked against whether it affects the core launch-now-vs-wait decision (cut if it's just flavor); balance was tuned to avoid snowballing (rising upgrade costs, discounts for players who fall behind); the team was explicit about not fabricating real rocket/instrument/mission data — approximated balance values are flagged as such in code/docs.

projectDetails.name: Project The Great Gig in the Sky
projectDetails.summary: Earth Jukebox makes NASA Earth science audible. It turns seven NASA Earth Information Center visualization sequences—near-surface temperature, wind, precipitation, specific humidity, PM2.5, ozone, and carbon monoxide—into browser-generated sound. Listeners can navigate with a keyboard and screen reader, choose the whole planet, a continent, or a country without relying on a mouse, move through frames, hear frame readings, and combine variables. An optional spoken guide for controls and a metronome support the listening experience. A jukebox-inspired interface gives each variable a distinct, repeatable sound mapping. The project offers blind and low-vision audiences another way to explore changing Earth patterns, while remaining open to everyone. The sounds follow documented rules applied to image-derived values; wind and PM2.5 use qualitative visual-signal indexes.
projectDetails.details:
Earth Jukebox turns seven NASA Earth Information Center visualization tracks into sound. The browser player decodes image colors using each visualization’s color scale, then maps image-derived values to musical notes, timbre, brightness, or rhythm using fixed rules. Tone.js synthesizes the sound live as the frames play.

Designed for keyboard navigation and screen readers, the experience lets listeners choose the whole planet, a continent, or a country without using a mouse. They can play or pause, move between frames, hear a frame’s readings, and combine variables in a separate mode. An optional spoken guide announces focused controls, and an optional metronome marks time intervals.

The jukebox concept turns Earth science into a collection of tracks to explore. It offers blind and low-vision audiences another way to engage with changing planetary patterns, while also inviting sighted visitors to listen.

The interface uses HTML, CSS, and JavaScript ES modules. The offline image-processing and evaluation pipeline uses Python, NumPy, Pillow, Requests, scikit-image, SciPy, imageio-ffmpeg, and Matplotlib. Natural Earth country boundaries support geographic selections.

The team considered how to keep the sound mappings consistent across places and time, make the controls usable without a mouse, and avoid implying more scientific certainty than the image-derived values support. Wind and PM2.5 use qualitative visual-signal indexes; their sounds do not represent direct measurements of wind speed or pollutant concentration. AI tools assisted with selected coding, data analysis, research, and documentation tasks; the team chose the project concept and sound mappings.

projectDetails.name: "TREM" DE FERRO: Minas Gerais Banded Iron Formations as Geochemical Analogs for Martian ISRU
projectDetails.summary: We developed an interactive web platform and in-situ resource utilization (ISRU) simulator, positioning the Banded Iron Formations (BIFs) of Brazil's Iron Quadrangle (Minas Gerais) as functional geochemical analogs for hematite-rich Martian regolith at Meridiani Planum and Gale Crater. Our solution moves beyond surface visual resemblances to terrestrial deserts by targeting mineral extraction. Based on the fundamental reduction reaction (2Fe₂O₃ → 4Fe + 3O₂), we model two mature metallurgical pathways Hydrogen Direct Reduction (H₂-DRI) and Molten Oxide Electrolysis (MOE) to co-produce breathable life-support oxygen, rocket propellant, and structural metallic iron for additive habitat manufacturing. This work addresses a primary constraint of deep space missions: return propellant (LOX) represents the single largest mass penalty from Earth (~25 metric tons for a four-person crew under NASA DRA 5.0). Testing these processing routes using Minas Gerais ores enables early calibration of specific energy consumption, chemical yields, and equipment reliability in terrestrial pilot facilities before launching payloads to Mars.
projectDetails.details:
"TREM" DE FERRO is an open-access web platform and ISRU simulator establishing a functional and geochemical bridge between terrestrial Banded Iron Formations (itabirites and hematites from Minas Gerais, Brazil) and Martian iron-oxide deposits identified by NASA rovers. Rather than seeking morphological desert analogs, we target chemical and mineral parity: extracting oxygen and metallic iron from ferric oxide (2Fe₂O₃ → 4Fe + 3O₂). The platform models two core industrial pathways: Hydrogen Direct Reduction (DRI-H₂), which thermochemically reduces ore into sponge iron and water vapor before recovering H₂ through water electrolysis, and Molten Oxide Electrolysis (MOE), which electrochemically cracks molten iron oxide at ~1,600 °C directly into pure liquid iron and gaseous oxygen without requiring water.

The primary benefit is substantially derisking surface operations and reducing launch mass. According to NASA’s Mars Design Reference Architecture 5.0 (DRA 5.0), return descent/ascent vehicles require approximately 25 metric tons of liquid oxygen (LOX). While NASA’s MOXIE experiment proved that atmospheric oxygen generation works, it produced 122 grams total throughout its mission. Sustained surface habitats require regolith mineral processing. By benchmarking processing routes in Minas Gerais pilot facilities, researchers can validate specific energy consumption (kWh/kg O₂), powder fluidization, and reduction kinetics on Earth prior to flight hardware fabrication.

The interactive platform was developed using React, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, and custom numerical models for stoichiometric and thermodynamic balances. Planetary datasets were retrieved from the NASA Planetary Data System (PDS) Geosciences and Atmospheres nodes, integrating APXS/CheMin spectrometry from Curiosity, PIXL data from Perseverance, Mössbauer hematite spectra from Opportunity, and MOXIE operational telemetry. Terrestrial geological grades and mineralogical baselines were sourced from CPRM/Geological Survey of Brazil (SGB) database surveys.

Our key conceptual shift was discarding passive landscape analogies in favor of active geochemical and metallurgical testing. Brazil possesses one of the world's most advanced mining and direct-reduction industrial ecosystems; mobilizing this infrastructure as an accessible proving ground for space exploration turns a major terrestrial industry into an operational asset for Mars.

The team established an explicit boundary for the analogy: what can be directly validated on Earth (dry magnetic pre-concentration efficiency, reduction kinetics, and thermodynamic efficiency) versus what strictly requires environmental simulation chambers (0.38 g Martian gravity, a 6 hPa CO₂ atmosphere, and reactive perchlorate salts in the regolith).

Far from home, the first astronauts to set foot on Mars will want the best map possible, with information on the details of their routes and destinations, updates on current conditions, and the data needed to complete their mission quickly and safely. Your challenge is to create a layered, integrated view of a location or route on the Martian surface that pulls together data from multiple NASA science missions and could help a human explorer plan and carry out a successful Marswalk while conducting new and exciting science along the way.

projectDetails.name: CrewVitals
projectDetails.summary: CrewVitals is a web app that lets an astronaut on a long mission check their own health in about a minute a day. The crew member logs six indicators: blood pressure, resting heart rate, blood glucose, body temperature, sleep and mood. The app compares each reading with a clinical reference range, shows a green, yellow or red status with plain-language guidance, tracks trends across mission days, and says when a result should go to the Crew Medical Officer or the flight surgeon on the ground. A clickable body map explains how spaceflight affects each body system, with every statement linked to its NASA source. A radiation panel compares dose rates measured by real instruments in six environments, from the International Space Station to the surface of Mars, and a banner reports recent solar events, all from NASA databases. On missions far from Earth, communication with the ground is delayed and crews carry much of the responsibility for noticing changes in their own health. CrewVitals is built for that situation.
projectDetails.details:
What it does

  • Daily check-in. One short form for six indicators, with a note beside each field on how to take the measurement. A status badge updates as the crew member types.
  • Dashboard. The mission day, an overall status, and one card per indicator with the reading, its position against the reference range, and what to do next.
  • Guidance and escalation. Green means keep the routine. Yellow gives self-care steps and asks for a new reading the next day. Red gives the next step for that indicator and says when to inform the Crew Medical Officer. A red trend goes to the Crew Medical Officer and the flight surgeon on the ground. A small set of critical values triggers an urgent message.
  • Trends. One chart per indicator across mission days, with the reference band shaded and out-of-range days marked. Four trend rules look at three consecutive days, for example sleep under six hours three nights in a row, and raise an alert that a single reading would not.
  • Body map. A figure with six regions. Selecting a region shows its latest readings, how spaceflight affects that body system, the related hazards of human spaceflight, related open-science studies, and the reason for tracking it.
  • Radiation across six environments. The radiation panel shows absorbed dose measured on the same day, 1 December 2022, by instruments on the ISS, in lunar orbit, inside the Orion capsule during Artemis I, in deep space, in Mars orbit and on the surface of Mars. The crew member can select each one to see its dose rate through the day. The panel states that the instruments differ in design, shielding and location, so the values are what each instrument measured and not comparable crew doses.
  • Space weather. A banner reports solar flares and solar energetic particle events from the last seven days.
  • Mission setting. The crew member chooses ISS, Lunar surface or Mars transit. On Mars transit, every instruction that sends the crew to the ground adds a reminder that communication is delayed and the onboard procedure comes first. The panel also says plainly where no measured data exists for the chosen setting.
  • Two languages. The app opens in English and can be switched to Brazilian Portuguese with one selector. Links to NASA pages are marked as English-language pages when the app is in Portuguese.
  • Demo mission. One button loads 30 days of simulated crew data, clearly labelled as simulated, so the trends and alerts can be seen at once.

How it works

CrewVitals is a single-page web app that runs in the browser. Health entries are stored only on the device, in the browser's local storage, and nothing the crew member types is sent to a server. Status rules and reference ranges live in one file, so a flight surgeon could review or replace them in one place. Three small server functions fetch NASA data and fall back to a saved copy when a source is unavailable. The app always shows whether NASA data is live or a saved snapshot, and always labels simulated crew data.

What we were careful about

  • The alert thresholds are adult clinical reference ranges used on Earth, and the app says so on every card. We did not invent spaceflight-specific thresholds. They were reviewed by the team's biomedical engineer.
  • NASA statements are paraphrased and shown with a link to the NASA page they come from. A team member checked each paraphrase against its NASA source. The team's own reasoning is shown separately and labelled as ours.
  • No environment is presented as another. There is no measured lunar-surface or Mars-transit radiation data in the source database, and the app says so instead of substituting a different environment.
  • Status is never shown by colour alone. Each status has an icon and a text label. An automated accessibility check reports no violations on any screen.
  • The app is a hackathon prototype and not a medical device, and it says so on every page.

Benefits and goals

On a Mars mission a message to the ground can take up to 20 minutes to arrive, and the answer as long to come back. A crew member needs a tool that helps them notice a change early, tells them what they can do themselves, and makes clear when to involve the crew's medical officer. Our goal was a tool simple enough to use every day and honest about what it knows. Next steps would be readings taken directly from onboard medical devices, thresholds set by flight surgeons, and a personal radiation dose record fed by the crew member's own dosimeter.

Tools and technologies

TypeScript, React, Vite, Tailwind CSS, Recharts, React Router, Lucide icons, Vitest. Hosted on Cloudflare Pages with Pages Functions. Source code: https://github.com/pedronogueira21/crewvitals

How we used NASA and partner data

  • NASA Human Research Program, "5 Hazards of Human Spaceflight": the frame for the whole app. Each indicator and body region is linked to the hazards that affect it.
  • NASA, "The Human Body in Space": source of the paraphrased statements in the body map.
  • NASA RadLab (Open Science Data Repository): absorbed dose rates for one common day, 1 December 2022, from six instruments: ISS (DosTel1), lunar orbit (LRO, CRaTER), inside Orion on Artemis I (HERA), deep space (BioSentinel, BPD), Mars orbit (TGO, Liulin-MO) and Mars surface (Curiosity, MSL-RAD).
  • NASA CCMC DONKI: recent solar flares and solar energetic particle events for the space-weather banner.
  • NASA Open Science Data Repository search: related open-science studies for each indicator, shown with organism and study type because many are animal or ground studies.
  • ESA: the Mars-orbit measurements come from the Liulin-MO dosimeter on the ExoMars Trace Gas Orbiter, a joint ESA–Roscosmos mission. We accessed them through NASA's RadLab database.
  • The alert ranges are adapted from ACC/AHA blood pressure categories and American Diabetes Association glucose criteria.

Use of AI

The application code was written with Claude Code (Anthropic) and reviewed and tested by the team. Claude also helped plan the project and drafted the interface text, the paraphrases of NASA pages (each checked by a team member against its source), the Portuguese translation and the demo slides. Gemini (Google) was used as an aid in the clinical review, which the team's biomedical engineer approved. The body map figure and the app icon are simple schematics drawn in code with AI assistance, identified as such in the app. The demo mission is simulated data and is labelled as simulated. No NASA logos or mission identifiers are used.

challengeDetails.title: Create Health Monitoring Software for Astronauts on Space Missions
challengeDetails.excerpt: Long-duration missions expose astronauts to space radiation, isolation and confinement, altered gravity, and a hostile closed environment, which can bring immune changes, bone loss, cardiovascular events, and behavioral health problems. On long missions, astronauts carry much of the responsibility for spotting these changes in themselves. Your challenge is to build a health monitoring software that gathers health indicators and enables astronauts to evaluate and act on the status of their health.

challengeDetails.excerpt: Understanding how burning activity is distributed across our planet over time, including wildfires and agricultural burns intense enough to be detected by satellite sensors, enables us to anticipate critical periods, guide monitoring efforts, and improve fire response.  Satellites have tracked active fire hotspots for more than two decades, but the record is split across sensors whose data cannot be compared directly, leaving fire managers without a consistent picture of when and where burning has occurred. Your challenge is to build a web application that harmonizes these records into a burning activity calendar based on active fire hotspots,  enabling early warning and emergency responders, scientists, and land managers to examine historical fire patterns, unusual conditions, and critical periods within a selected area of interest.

projectDetails.name: Project Ares
projectDetails.summary:
Project Ares is a pixel-art game, in Portuguese and English, where children aged 7 to 12 command a mission to Mars: a 180-day journey and 10 sols at the base. Each turn, players split limited energy (8 points, only 4 during a dust storm) among air and water, greenhouse, radiation shield and radio, which sends science to Earth (goal: 30). Decision cards offer two options, and both have a cost; the active option leads to a 15-second minigame. Crew members Lia, Davi and Yara have their own bonuses, and the robot Orbi guides the tutorial. The ending is punishment-free: a 1-to-3-star debriefing and a certificate with the player’s name.

The game answers the challenge of teaching real space engineering decisions to young learners: energy is limited and every system competes for the same resources. It uses real NASA data: radiation measured by the Curiosity rover and 1,036 solar flares from 2024 in the DONKI archive. The storm warning only arrives with the radio on, forcing a choice between science and safety. The data is archived and shown with its date and source. The game rules are separate from the interface and covered by automated tests.

It matters because children learn through consequences: they discover why radiation is the biggest obstacle on the way to Mars and how engineers decide under uncertainty. It is free, bilingual, accessible (keyboard, screen reader, optional minigames) and runs in any browser, reaching schools and families at no cost.
projectDetails.details:
Project Ares is an interactive, bilingual educational browser game that simulates the challenges of a human mission to Mars. Designed for children aged 7 to 12, it combines pixel-art visuals, storytelling, resource management, and interactive minigames to make space science more engaging and accessible.

How It Works

Players take command of a three-member astronaut crew: Lia, the commander; Davi, the engineer; and Yara, the botanist. Each character has a unique bonus, while Orbi, a companion robot, guides players through the tutorial and provides contextual hints throughout the experience.

The gameplay is divided into two phases: a 180-day journey to Mars, represented by six turns, followed by ten Martian sols at the base. During each turn, players manage a limited energy supply generated by solar panels, allocating resources among four essential systems: air and water, greenhouse food production, radiation protection, and radio communications. Players must balance crew survival with scientific research, aiming to transmit 30 science points back to Earth.

Random events introduce additional challenges through decision cards with two possible outcomes. Each active decision leads to a short minigame that can improve or worsen its result. The experience concludes with a non-punitive performance assessment, encouraging players to learn from their decisions and try again.

Benefits and Intended Impact

Project Ares promotes scientific literacy, critical thinking, strategic planning, and resource management. Rather than presenting space science through passive explanations, it allows children to understand scientific concepts through consequences and experimentation.

The game incorporates authentic NASA information, including radiation measurements collected by the Curiosity rover, solar flare records from NASA's DONKI database, and references to real technologies and missions such as the ISS water recycling system, Perseverance's MOXIE experiment, and the Opportunity rover.

This approach helps children understand the real difficulties of space exploration, particularly radiation exposure, environmental hazards, energy limitations, and the importance of scientific communication. The intended impact is to encourage curiosity about science, technology, engineering, and space exploration from an early age.

Technologies and Development Tools

The project was developed using:

  • HTML5: Page structure and game interface.
  • CSS3: Visual design, pixel-art presentation, animations, and responsive layouts.
  • JavaScript: Gameplay mechanics, resource management, event systems, character bonuses, and minigames.
  • Python: Data collection and processing scripts for NASA datasets.
  • Node.js Test Runner: Approximately 25 automated tests covering the core game logic.
  • Vercel: Deployment and hosting, providing public access to the game.
  • NASA Open Data: Scientific datasets and mission information used to support gameplay accuracy.
  • Git and GitHub: Version control, source code management, and collaborative development.

GitHub Repository: https://github.com/germanoafb/Base_Mars

The architecture separates the game rules from the user interface, making the system easier to maintain, test, and expand. The game runs directly in the browser without requiring installation.

Creativity and Innovation

The creative aspect of Project Ares lies in transforming complex scientific information into meaningful gameplay mechanics. Radiation exposure, solar storms, energy scarcity, and scientific communication are not merely background details; they directly influence player decisions and mission outcomes.

For example, maintaining radio communications allows players to receive early warnings about solar storms, creating a strategic trade-off between scientific progress and crew safety. Similarly, radiation protection requires careful resource allocation, demonstrating why shielding is essential for long-duration space missions.

The combination of pixel-art aesthetics, character-driven storytelling, interactive minigames, and real scientific data creates an educational experience that connects entertainment with authentic scientific challenges.

Factors Considered During Development

The team considered several important factors:

  • Scientific accuracy: NASA data is presented with its original dates and sources, without being misrepresented as real-time information.
  • Age-appropriate design: Mechanics, language, and visual elements are designed for children aged 7–12.
  • Accessibility: Keyboard navigation, screen-reader compatibility, reduced-motion support, and the ability to skip minigames.
  • Educational value: Every major gameplay mechanic reinforces a scientific concept or encourages strategic thinking.
  • Fairness and engagement: The non-punitive ending encourages experimentation and learning rather than discouraging players for making mistakes.
  • Accessibility of technology: Free hosting, browser compatibility, and bilingual support make the experience available to schools and families without additional costs.

Ultimately, Project Ares aims to demonstrate that scientific education can be interactive, inclusive, and entertaining while remaining grounded in real-world research. It invites children to experience the challenges of Mars exploration and inspires them to think like scientists, engineers, and explorers.

challengeDetails.title: Build a Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer
challengeDetails.excerpt: Space-themed STEM content often oversimplifies the engineering trade-offs that define a real mission or presents them at a level too complex to hold a young learner's attention. Few tools make those trade-offs both tangible and fun. Your challenge is to design and build an interactive game or app that lets students run a lunar or Martian outpost, balancing competing demands like life support, radiation shielding, power, and food production, so they experience firsthand the decisions that determine whether a mission fails or succeeds.

projectDetails.name: Project XBigDevs
projectDetails.summary:
Mars Route Planner (MRP) is a web app for planning a Marswalk (EVA) in Jezero crater. The astronaut marks a start point and science stops on a map built from several NASA missions (MRO HiRISE and CTX, Mars Odyssey THEMIS, MGS MOLA). The app computes a safe route over the real relief, avoiding slopes of 25° and more, and estimates the time and oxygen with a walking model scaled to Mars gravity. The EVA can be replayed in 2D or 3D.

The challenge asks for an integrated, layered view of one Martian site that answers three questions. MRP shows where to go and at what cost, comparing the return to the habitat and to the start. It shows current conditions from the latest Perseverance MEDA data. It also highlights which science targets are worth visiting and which mission revealed each one.

On Mars, a bad route can mean running out of oxygen. MRP gives a GO / NO-GO verdict with a 10% O₂ reserve and marks the point of no return. Every layer cites its mission and date, and every estimate is labeled as one, so planners can trust what they see.
projectDetails.details:
Mars Route Planner (MRP) is a web app for planning a Marswalk in Jezero crater. The astronaut marks a start point and science stops on a map built from NASA mission data (MRO HiRISE and CTX, Mars Odyssey THEMIS, MGS MOLA). An A* algorithm then finds a safe route over the real terrain, avoiding slopes of 25° and more. A walking model scaled to Mars gravity estimates the time and oxygen of each plan. With the 0.73 kg of oxygen of NASA’s lunar suit design and a 10% reserve, the app gives a GO / NO-GO verdict for returning to the habitat or to the start. It also marks the point of no return and can reorder the stops to save oxygen. The EVA can be replayed in 2D or 3D, and a Conditions screen shows the latest Perseverance MEDA weather data.

Its main benefit is making the most critical limit visible before going outside: will the oxygen last? Every layer cites its mission and date, and every estimate is labeled as one, so planners know what is measured and what is modeled.

We built it with TypeScript, React, Leaflet and CesiumJS, and processed the NASA data with Python. It is a static site on Cloudflare, so it runs on any browser, including phones. Its creative core is turning a route into a survival decision, while staying transparent about every assumption.

This project is an MVP, ready to expand by processing more data. The Python pipeline turns NASA rasters into light files with a fixed format, and the routing engine works on any grid in that format. Adding new landing sites, finer terrain, more map layers or a longer MEDA weather history means running the pipeline on new data, not rewriting the app.
